hiro_okonomiyaki_sakuramaru.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The signature dishes feature Miyajima oysters, pork, egg, and seafood, and Hiroshima okonomiyaki standardly includes egg, meat, and bonito/fish-based sauce and dashi. No vegan options are documented.
hiro_okonomiyaki_sakuramaru.hours_raw: 11:00-16:00 (last order around 15:00-15:30). Wednesday closed; occasionally also closed on some Fridays / irregular closures.
hiro_okonomiyaki_sakuramaru.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki shop sitting along the Omotesando approach on Miyajima, a short walk from the ferry terminal toward Itsukushima Shrine. It is an intimate counter-and-tatami spot built around the everyday foods Hiroshima locals grew up on. (Map pin approximate — Omotesandō; use the Maps link for exact spot.)

chef_bio.background: A small Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki shop sitting along the Omotesando approach on Miyajima, a short walk from the ferry terminal toward Itsukushima Shrine. It is an intimate counter-and-tatami spot (about 20 seats) built around the everyday foods Hiroshima locals grew up on.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop frames a trip as the pairing of beautiful scenery and good food, inviting visitors to enjoy Hiroshima's down-to-earth comfort dishes - okonomiyaki and oysters - side by side.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki topped with oysters harvested in the waters off Miyajima, layered with the region's characteristic thin noodles, plus foil-grilled oyster dishes.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen grills oysters caught off Miyajima right on the teppan and sets them atop the okonomiyaki, billing it as a way to taste Hiroshima's and Miyajima's local specialties in one dish.
The Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki here is built with notably thin noodles, layering batter, vegetables, meat, noodles and egg before being pressed and steamed on the griddle.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site and gorp.jp confirm Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki with slightly thinner noodles, Miyajima-harvested oysters grilled on the teppan and placed atop the okonomiyaki, foil-grilled oysters, about 20 counter/tatami seats, and the 'beautiful scenery and delicious food' message.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat-based okonomiyaki batter and wheat noodles are cooked on a shared teppan griddle alongside all dishes, so a gluten-free meal is not feasible here.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No allergen labeling is published; okonomiyaki sauce and seasonings are standardly wheat-containing and no gluten-free alternative is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Oysters, pork, egg and other seafood are central to the menu and share the same griddle; no vegan preparation is documented.

positives.text: An English menu is available, which can help a traveler ask about ingredients.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu is available and the shop is used to tourists, so a foreign student can order comfortably without much Japanese.

hiro_hiroshima_kinchaiya.vegan_detail: The okonomiyaki uses egg, pork, squid tempura, and bonito/fish-based dashi and toppings, and teppanyaki centers on meat and seafood. No vegan dishes are documented.

chef_bio.background: A compact, owner-run okonomiyaki and teppanyaki counter that opened on August 23, 2023, tucked back from the street in the Ginzan-cho area of central Hiroshima. The shop seats just six at a single counter facing the griddle, where the friendly owner cooks and keeps up easy conversation with guests.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki layered with fine noodles, plus a range of teppanyaki. A signature plate is the 'Kinchai no Meigetsu Soba,' topped with squid tempura, shredded nori, and a sunny-side egg.

anecdotes.text: Regulars describe the owner as a relaxed, likable guy who deftly works the small griddle and chats with everyone seated at the counter.
Because the storefront sits set back from the street, visitors are advised to watch for the shop's sign so they don't walk past it.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The modokimaru review and Tabelog confirm an August 23, 2023 opening in Naka-ku's Ginzan-cho, six counter seats set back from the street, a friendly owner, and the 'Kinchai no Meigetsu Soba' (¥1,580) with squid tempura, seasoned nori and a firmed egg.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny six-seat counter run solo by a friendly owner who chats with guests while he cooks; no English documented, so a little Japanese or a translation app will help a foreign student feel at ease.

hiro_hiroshima_kaki_miyamae.vegan_detail: This is an oyster and seafood izakaya whose core dishes are oysters, conger eel (anago), small sardines, and A5 wagyu, with fish/shellfish and wheat-soy seasoning throughout. No vegan menu or vegan accommodation is documented.

hiro_hiroshima_kaki_miyamae.notes: [Mom & Pop] An at-home, owner-run Seto Inland Sea cuisine spot in central Hiroshima built around the region's signature ingredient: oysters from the bay that lands the most oysters in Japan, brought in daily from the local market.

chef_bio.background: An at-home, owner-run Seto Inland Sea cuisine spot in central Hiroshima (Nakamachi, near Fukuromachi) built around the region's signature ingredient: oysters from the area that lands the most oysters in Japan, brought in daily from the local market.
chef_bio.philosophy: Let guests taste the best of Hiroshima in one homey room, sourcing seafood directly and stocking around 30 local sakes including brewery-direct and seasonal limited bottles.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima brand 'Kaki Komachi' oysters (large, over 150g) served raw, grilled, or fried; white-grilled local anago; small sardines; teppanyaki; and A5 wagyu, paired with a deep local-sake list.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen prides itself on a lineup of roughly 30 local sakes, including brewery-sourced and seasonal limited bottles, to pair with the oysters.
Signature 'Kaki Komachi' oysters can be ordered raw, grilled, or as kaki fry, with multi-course menus showcasing Hiroshima specialties.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site, HotPepper and Tabelog confirm 'Kaki Komachi' oysters exceeding 150g served raw/grilled/fried, white-grilled anago, teppanyaki, A5 wagyu, roughly 30 local sakes, and oysters sourced daily from Hiroshima's market, Japan's largest for oyster landings.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes are seasoned in the standard Japanese izakaya style; soy-sauce-based seasonings contain wheat, and fried oysters (kaki fry) use a wheat batter/breading.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is centered on oysters, anago, sardines and other seafood plus wagyu, so animal products are pervasive across the menu.

cultural_comfort.note: A homey, small owner-run izakaya where a few words of Japanese and a willingness to point at the menu will go a long way; no indication of English support.

hiro_tetta.gf_detail: This is a Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki and teppanyaki house. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
hiro_tetta.vegan_detail: A meat-and-seafood teppanyaki/okonomiyaki counter: signature dishes include uni-horen (sea urchin and spinach), egg-rich okonomiyaki, and black Wagyu offal, and sauces contain fish/wheat-based ingredients. No vegan options are documented.
hiro_tetta.hours_raw: 18:00-03:00 (L.O. 02:30) daily, per the operator's HotPepper listing (no regular holiday). Tabelog lists 18:00-02:00 with Sundays/day-after-holidays closed; the operator page shows open year-round.

chef_bio.background: A long-running Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki and teppanyaki counter in the Yakenbori nightlife quarter, where everything is cooked on the iron griddle right in front of you at a small counter. The kitchen leans on carefully chosen Hiroshima ingredients, and the okonomiyaki noodles are coated in a house-made dashi and griddled slowly for over ten minutes so the outside turns crisp while the inside stays moist.
chef_bio.philosophy: Make the most of select local ingredients and cook each okonomiyaki slowly and properly rather than fast.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, plus the local favorite uni-horen (sea urchin and spinach) on the teppan and black Wagyu offal.

anecdotes.text: The signature uni-horen (sea urchin with spinach) drew wider attention after being featured on television.
Regulars keep coming back in part for the easygoing owner, who chats with guests across the counter as he cooks.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: HotPepper confirms a Yakenbori counter shop cooking on the teppan, house-made dashi noodles griddled over ten minutes for a crisp outside and moist inside, uni-horen (¥1,700) featured on TV, black wagyu offal, exclusively Hiroshima-sourced ingredients, and an engaging owner.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A single shared teppan griddle is used for all dishes, including wheat-batter okonomiyaki and noodles, so heavy gluten cross-contact is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes are finished with okonomiyaki/soy-style sauces that are typically wheat-based; no gluten-free sauce is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The griddle is used for meat, seafood (sea urchin), egg and Wagyu offal, so any item would share surfaces with animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny counter-only local spot where the owner chats with guests in Japanese and there is no English menu or website, so a little Japanese (or a translation app) makes the visit much smoother.

hiro_teppanyaki_okonomiyaki_m.gf_detail: Okonomiyaki batter is wheat-based and not gluten-free, and teppanyaki dishes are typically finished with wheat-containing soy sauce or sauces. There is no documented gluten-free menu or handling, so this is not suitable for strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_teppanyaki_okonomiyaki_m.vegan_detail: The menu centers on egg, bacon, butter, and other meat/seafood teppanyaki and okonomiyaki dishes; the signature omurice uses egg and bacon, and sauces rely on fish/soy bases. No documented vegan options.

chef_bio.background: A family-run teppanyaki and okonomiyaki counter that built its reputation over 18 years on Ebisu-dori (胡子通り) before relocating about eight years ago to its current spot in the Nagarekawa area of central Hiroshima. Through the move it has kept the same intimate, family feel and a loyal following.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki and teppanyaki, with a much-loved fluffy omurice (omelette rice with bacon, onion, ketchup rice, and a finish of melted butter) as the standout signature dish. The owner is especially known for deft work with butter on the griddle.

anecdotes.text: Regulars rave about a simple scallion dish, with one diner saying they had never eaten such delicious scallions before.
Visitors are often surprised to find such consistently delicious cooking tucked away here, with a common refrain that everything on the menu is good.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog confirms 18 years on Ebisu-dori before relocating about eight years ago to the Nagarekawa area, the family-run feel, a signature omurice with ketchup rice, bacon and onion finished with melted butter, the owner's butter skill, and a much-praised scallion dish.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a small, late-night family-run teppanyaki counter where ordering is in Japanese; a few basic phrases or a translation app will help, and the warm owner makes it welcoming once you're seated.

No dedicated gluten-free preparation or allergy handling is mentioned.
hiro_hiroshima_kaki_miyamae_h.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The restaurant is an oyster and seafood izakaya — signature dishes are raw and grilled oysters, anago, small sardines and wagyu beef. No vegan or plant-based menu is documented.
hiro_hiroshima_kaki_miyamae_h.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Thu-Sun & holidays 17:00-23:00 (last order 22:00). Closed Wednesdays. Weekends/holidays may use 2-hour time-limited staggered seatings.
hiro_hiroshima_kaki_miyamae_h.notes: [Mom & Pop] A sister branch (離れ) of the original 廣島牡蠣 みやまえ, this small Seto Inland Sea izakaya sits on Jizo-dori in Komachi, a short walk from Chuden-mae and within the Peace Park area of central Hiroshima.

chef_bio.background: A sister branch (離れ) of the original 廣島牡蠣 みやまえ, this small Seto Inland Sea izakaya sits on Jizo-dori in Komachi, a short walk from Chuden-mae in central Hiroshima.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner sources oysters daily directly from Hiroshima's market — Japan's largest for oyster landings — and procures high-quality meat through his own channels to offer it at reasonable prices, while personally curating the sake selection.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima brand oysters served raw and grilled, alongside white-grilled anago (conger eel), small sardines, A5 wagyu steak and teppanyaki, paired with a curated lineup of around 30 local sake.

anecdotes.text: Oysters are brought in fresh each day from Hiroshima's market, which has the highest oyster landing volume in Japan.
The same owner, Asayama Ikuya, runs both the original 廣島牡蠣 みやまえ and this 離れ.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official sites, HotPepper and Tabelog (plus search) confirm owner Asayama Ikuya operates both branches; the 離れ sits in Komachi on Jizo-dori near Chuden-mae, serving Kaki Komachi oysters (raw/grilled), white-grilled anago, A5 wagyu sourced through the owner's channels, and about 30 curated local sakes.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Menu is built on oysters, white-grilled anago, small sardines and teppanyaki, which in Japanese cooking typically use wheat-based soy sauce and seasonings; no gluten-free preparation is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is a seafood and oyster izakaya with no documented vegan or plant-based dishes; cross-contact with fish and shellfish should be expected throughout the kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, dinner-only local oyster izakaya where some Japanese helps; reservations are made through Japanese booking sites, so a foreign student may want a Japanese-speaking friend or translation app to book and order comfortably.

hiro_chuka_soba_maru_funairi_.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop. The chuka soba and chashu-men use wheat noodles in a soy-seasoned broth (soy sauce contains wheat), so there are no gluten-free options. Not suitable for gluten-free or celiac diners.
hiro_chuka_soba_maru_funairi_.vegan_detail: The broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu/soy) base and dishes are topped with chashu pork; this is a meat-based ramen specialist with no vegan menu. Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
hiro_chuka_soba_maru_funairi_.notes: [Mom & Pop] A long-running Hiroshima chuka soba shop. The current proprietor inherited the recipe and approach from the previous owner of the Funairi location and reopened it after renovation in February 2020, continuing a flavor that locals have known since childhood.

chef_bio.background: A long-running Hiroshima chuka soba shop. The current proprietor inherited the recipe and approach from the previous owner of the Funairi location and reopened it after renovation in February 2020, continuing a flavor that locals have known since childhood.
chef_bio.philosophy: Preserve the nostalgic, time-honored taste and pass it to future generations while welcoming families warmly with a smile.
chef_bio.specialty: Traditional Hiroshima-style chuka soba: thin noodles in a soy-seasoned pork-bone broth, served simply (chuka soba 750 yen, chashu-men 850 yen).

anecdotes.text: The owner describes wanting to keep sharing 'that flavor familiar since childhood' with as many customers as possible for years to come, welcoming everyone with a smile.
Reopened in February 2020 after renovation, with the current owner inheriting the previous Funairi proprietor's recipe.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: mypl.net and Tabelog confirm the current owner took over from the previous Funairi proprietor and relaunched in February 2020 after renovation, serving a nostalgic soy pork-bone chuka soba with thin noodles and bean sprouts (chuka soba ¥750, chashu-men ¥850).

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth and seasoning are soy-sauce based; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and the noodles are wheat noodles.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 12-seat counter ramen shop with no English support and cash only, so come with the dish name written down and exact change ready.

hiro_niku_no_masui.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. This is a butcher-run meat restaurant whose entire identity is beef sukiyaki, pork cutlets, beef cutlets, and other meat dishes; no vegan options are documented.

chef_bio.background: A meat shop that opened a dining room in 1956, during the years Hiroshima was rebuilding after the war. Decades on it is still run as a family meat business (精肉店直営) with a restaurant attached, beloved by locals as one of the city's classic yoshoku (Japanese-style Western food) institutions, spread across two floors that fill with a lunchtime crowd.
chef_bio.philosophy: A reporter described the kindness and warmth of the place: the most popular dish is prepared ahead so customers barely have to wait, a small everyday courtesy that keeps regulars coming back.
chef_bio.specialty: Service tonkatsu — a thin, crisp pork cutlet served almost the moment you order it, generously coated in the house sauce (around 380 yen with rice) — alongside carefully prepared beef sukiyaki, where staff grill premium marbled loin at just the right temperature. As a butcher-run kitchen, the restaurant trades on the quality and value of its meat.

anecdotes.text: The signature service tonkatsu has been famous for being remarkably cheap and quick — a thin, crispy cutlet with rice (about 380 yen) that arrives with almost no wait because it is prepared in advance.

Opened in 1956 ('Showa 31'), the same year as the famous economic line 'the post-war era is over,' the meat-shop restaurant became a local favorite known above all for its sukiyaki, with waitresses grilling beautifully marbled beef tableside.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hread.home-tv, gotrip and mrs.living confirm a 1956 (Showa 31) founding as a meat-shop-run (精肉店直営) yoshoku restaurant in Hatchobori, a ¥380 service tonkatsu (originally devised for cash-strapped students) prepared in advance, tableside sukiyaki with marbled beef, and a two-floor layout busy at lunch.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Tonkatsu and other fried cutlets are breaded in wheat flour and panko and deep-fried; frying oil is shared across breaded items, so heavy cross-contact with gluten is expected.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes such as sukiyaki and Western-style preparations use standard Japanese soy sauce and sauces, which contain wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: This is a meat-focused, butcher-run restaurant where nearly every dish centers on beef or pork; no vegan or plant-based items are documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, casual local institution where ordering is easiest with a few Japanese words or by pointing at the menu; staff are warm but English is limited, so a translation app helps.

hiro_tonkatsu_tonki.gf_detail: This is a tonkatsu specialist: the pork cutlets are breaded in wheat flour and panko (breadcrumbs), and the house tonkatsu sauce is not gluten-free. There is no indication of any gluten-free preparation, and the menu is built around fried, breaded items, so it is not suitable for someone requiring gluten-free.
hiro_tonkatsu_tonki.vegan_detail: A pork-cutlet specialty restaurant. Core dishes are deep-fried pork; the frying oil is 100% lard, and the standard set includes pork soup (tonjiru). There are no documented vegan options, and the shop is not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
hiro_tonkatsu_tonki.hours_raw: Mon–Sat 11:00–14:00 (L.O. 14:00) and 17:30–20:00 (L.O. 19:30); closed Sundays, holidays, and days adjacent to holidays. (A separate local listing notes 11:00–15:00 / 17:30–21:00; lunch and dinner service confirmed.)
hiro_tonkatsu_tonki.notes: [Mom & Pop] A long-running tonkatsu shop in Hiroshima's Minami Ward that opened in 1981 and has become so well known locally that, as one feature put it, in Hiroshima 'tonkatsu means Tonki.' chef_bio.background: A long-running tonkatsu shop in Hiroshima's Minami Ward that opened around 1981 (roughly 45 years in business) and has become so well known locally that, as one feature put it, in Hiroshima 'tonkatsu means Tonki.' It is a small, independently run shop on a counter-centered floor that nonetheless opens into a surprisingly deep interior with tables and a tatami room. A related shop in the Nishi Ward area exists as a branch-off (noren-wake).
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner describes aiming for 'food I myself find delicious — something anyone who eats it will think is delicious' (自分が食べておいしいもの。誰が食べてもおいしいと思ってもらえるようなものを目指しています).
chef_bio.specialty: Loin tonkatsu set (roasu katsu teishoku), with thick, tender cutlets, a homemade sauce, shredded cabbage with a choice of two dressings, hearty pork soup, pickles and orange. First refills of rice and pork soup are free.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen rotates four separate oil pots so the oil can rest between uses for a crisper fry, and avoids crowding cutlets to keep the oil temperature steady; the frying oil is 100% lard to concentrate umami.
Sauce and breadcrumbs are made in-house, and the shop is calm and tidy with a counter that makes it comfortable to visit alone.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hread.home-tv and mypl.net confirm a Minami-ku shop about 45 years old (opened ~1981), the 'tonkatsu means Tonki' reputation, four rotated oil pots, 100% lard frying oil, house-made sauce and breadcrumbs, a loin katsu set with free first refills, and a Nishi-ku noren-wake branch. The owner's personal name is not published in the sources.

gf_cross_contamination.text: All cutlets are coated in wheat flour and panko and deep-fried, so the shared fryers carry gluten; no gluten-free preparation is indicated.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: House tonkatsu sauce is used on the cutlets; tonkatsu sauce is wheat-based and not gluten-free.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Frying oil is 100% lard (pork fat), so all fried items are cooked in animal fat; the set also includes pork soup.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, traditional local tonkatsu shop with counter seating where you can comfortably eat alone, but staff likely speak mostly Japanese and there may be no English menu, so a few basic Japanese phrases or a translation app will help.

hiro_ichigakusho_mikansei.gf_detail: No gluten-free claims are documented anywhere. The curry roux is made without oil but there is no information confirming it is wheat-free, and Japanese curry roux commonly contains wheat flour as a thickener. A gluten-free traveler would need to ask directly about each dish; treat as not confirmed GF.

However, the signature and most popular dish is a tandoori chicken curry, and the evening menu includes general izakaya items and alcohol, so this is not a vegetarian/vegan establishment. A vegetable-based curry appears to be available, but ingredients (dairy, stock, honey/fruit) are not documented as vegan. A vegan diner should ask whether a specific curry can be made without animal products.

chef_bio.origin: Hiroshima (central Naka-ku, Kamiyacho, near the Hondori shopping street and Peace Memorial Park area)
chef_bio.background: The cafe grew out of a classical-music kissaten the owner first opened about 30 years ago. After running that earlier room for some 22 years she reinvented the concept, drawing on her food-industry experience to make curry the centerpiece, and in 2013 moved to a larger space near Hondori (Kamiyacho) so she could finally combine the two things she loves most.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner's playful motto is that the most delicious curry is the one made at home, so she sets out to make 'the second most delicious' - cooked daily with care and kept fresh rather than aged. The bigger dream realized in the current space was to let people enjoy real curry and live classical music together, casually, without needing a concert hall.
chef_bio.specialty: Oil-free homemade curry simmered from vegetables, fruits, and spices; a much-loved version is a generous chicken curry.

anecdotes.text: Lunchtimes sometimes feature live piano and violin, and the evening occasionally turns into a mini-concert with performers, spotlights and all - the room is built around a grand piano, cello, and contrabass.
A signature quirk is the no-oil cooking; the curry is prepared without any added fat, which is why regulars describe it as an unusually 'healthy' curry.
Beyond the standards there are playful options such as a banana curry, reflecting the fruit-and-vegetable base of the recipes.

positives.text: The curry is cooked without any oil/fat, using a base of vegetables, fruits, and spices, which can suit health-conscious and lighter-eating diners.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed adult salon-style cafe where classical music and curry mix; staff are described as friendly and chatty, but expect a mostly Japanese-speaking setting, so a few basic phrases will help.

chef_bio.background: Resort opened in 1975 in Hiroshima's Fukuro-machi district, founded by Numaguchi Tadashi together with three friends. After a period of closure, it was revived in 2014 at its current Tatemachi address, where it sits a short walk from the Hondori shopping arcade and the Nakanotana market street.
chef_bio.philosophy: The family wants the gratin to taste creamy and gentle so it is loved by children and adults alike, and to carry the historic shop forward to the next generation while adapting to the times.
chef_bio.specialty: Rice gratin (raisu guratan) baked piping hot in custom lidless ovens, topped with creamy bechamel and cheese grated fresh from whole blocks. Beloved varieties include Monaco (tomato/ketchup rice with chicken), Oscar (butter rice with shrimp) and Andre (curry-flavored rice with clams), plus shrimp cream croquettes and a homemade onion salad.

anecdotes.text: The founder and his daughter's husband, Yoshikawa Hirohito, led the revival; Yoshikawa said he did not want to let such a historic shop come to an end, and aims to grow Resort so it can be passed to the next generation.

chef_bio.background: Tsuta is a long-running, independent old-style café (junkissa) in central Hiroshima's Otemachi district, a short walk from the Shiyakusho-mae tram stop and near the Peace Memorial Park area. The blog author recalls coming here as a 'reward' during university days, calling the food that good.

While there are some plant-forward items (the signature bean aspic appetizer, soy-milk tofu, soy-milk hot pot, taro croquettes), the kitchen is not set up for vegan dining and a fully plant-based meal is not offered.

chef_bio.philosophy: Showcasing the virtues of Japanese washoku and fermentation culture (日本の和食、発酵文化の良さ), turning everyday ingredients into refined seasonal dishes.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal Japanese kaiseki built around fish and shellfish and a signature emphasis on bean dishes — the bean-aspic appetizer is repeatedly singled out as the highlight — alongside soy-milk tofu and other vegetable preparations. anecdotes.text: The signature opening dish, a bean aspic (豆のジュレ寄せ), is repeatedly called the best bite of the meal, and the menu leans into beans and soy-milk tofu throughout.
Because one chef cooks and serves everyone alone, the house offers a generous three-hour all-you-can-drink format so guests are never rushed despite the solo pace.
The place evolved from the 笹組 group and was formerly run as 豆と根菜 いし井 before its current incarnation.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Documented courses include soba noodles, tempura/fried items and anago (eel), all typical wheat and gluten sources in a shared kappo kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Cuisine is traditional Japanese washoku seasoned with standard soy sauce and dashi, which contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a small, solo-run counter restaurant where Japanese is the working language and reservations are essentially expected, so a foreign student will be most comfortable with some basic Japanese or a Japanese-speaking companion.

chef_bio.background: A neighborhood okonomiyaki shop founded in 1962 (Showa 37) on Jizo-dori, a downtown shopping street in Naka-ku that locals describe as a 'shitamachi within the city.' It has operated in the same spot for over half a century and is now run by Miho Matsuoka, the third-generation owner, who says she has been cooking her own okonomiyaki here since she was in elementary school. The shop got a light refresh in 2024 but keeps its Showa-era feel, with vintage photographs of its history on the walls.
chef_bio.philosophy: Matsuoka calls her approach 'subtraction okonomiyaki' (引き算のお好み焼き): she goes easy on fish powder, salt, and tenkasu so the dish comes together as one soft, unified bite rather than a pile of toppings. When she asked her founder grandmother for the batter recipe, the answer was 'there's no such thing -- you just feel it,' which pushed her to mix the batter by sense, adjusting for the day's temperature and water.
chef_bio.specialty: Rustic Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, especially 肉玉そば (pork-egg with soba noodles) and 肉玉うどん (with udon), with toppings kept deliberately minimal -- essentially just squid tempura (イカ天) and green onion.

anecdotes.text: Matsuoka personally walks to the greengrocer to buy cabbage and bean sprouts, touching each one to check quality, then carefully draws out the bitterness (aku) before cooking.
In 2020 she launched a mail-order frozen okonomiyaki line, cooking each piece herself at the factory, saying she wants people to remember 'not our name, but our taste.'
The shop has been recommended on television by comedian and self-styled gourmet Watabe Ken as a Hiroshima okonomiyaki spot worth seeking out, with the niku-tama udon singled out for its soft texture.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Cooked on a shared teppan grill where wheat-batter okonomiyaki and wheat noodles are prepared; no gluten-free handling is mentioned.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Uses a sweet okonomiyaki-style sauce (described as a 大福ソース-type sauce), which is wheat-based and not gluten-free.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a tiny, old-school counter-only neighborhood shop run by the family with no English menu expected, so basic Japanese or a translation app and patience will help a foreign student feel welcome.

chef_bio.background: A Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki and teppanyaki house in the heart of central Hiroshima (Otemachi), a short walk from the city's central avenues and the Peace Memorial Park area. Signature plates include sea urchin sauteed with buttered spinach (uni-horen), crispy teppan potato salad, oysters, A5 sirloin steak, and a griddled hotcake with ice cream to finish, paired with a well-chosen lineup of local Hiroshima sake.

anecdotes.text: The dining room is styled after a sake brewery, with private horigotatsu rooms that each have their own built-in griddle so food is cooked and served hot at the table.
The kitchen leans on Hiroshima and Seto Inland Sea ingredients, from local beef and oysters to a signature sea-urchin-and-spinach plate, matched with regional sake.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Teppanyaki and okonomiyaki here use standard wheat-based okonomi sauce and regular soy sauce; no wheat-free or tamari soy sauce is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed local okonomiyaki and teppanyaki house where a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will get you a warm welcome, though detailed dietary requests may be hard to communicate; note you must be 20 or older to enter.

hiro_tempura_suehiro.vegan_detail: The set meals and most plates include shrimp, squid, fish (mackerel), and chicken, and even vegetable tempura is fried in shared oil alongside seafood/meat and served with fish-based broth and sauces. There are vegetable tempura items on the menu (eggplant, pumpkin, mushroom), but they are not prepared vegan and there is no dedicated vegan offering. Not a vegan destination.
hiro_tempura_suehiro.notes: Tempura Suehiro opened in December 2020 in central Hiroshima's Nakamachi district, a short walk from Hondori and the Peace Park area. It pitches a modern, casual take on tempura — affordable enough for an everyday lunch yet served in a clean, refined wooden space.

chef_bio.background: Tempura Suehiro opened in December 2020 in central Hiroshima's Nakamachi district, a short walk from Hondori and the Peace Park area. It pitches a modern, casual take on tempura — affordable enough for an everyday lunch yet served in a clean, refined wooden space.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house proposes 'a new style of enjoying tempura' — pairing just-fried tempura with sake and wine in an izakaya-like, approachable setting rather than as formal haute cuisine. Each item is fried to order in front of the guest and brought to the counter on individual mesh trays as soon as it is done, so it arrives at peak crispness.
chef_bio.specialty: Freshly fried tempura served one piece at a time. The signature Suehiro Teishoku is a generous set of seven tempura items (shrimp, squid, mackerel, chicken, and three vegetables — eggplant, pumpkin, mushroom) with rice, miso soup, and pickles, plus free rice refills.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen serves tempura piece by piece on individual mesh draining trays so each item reaches the diner at maximum crispness, and the affordable teishoku comes with free rice refills (up to three bowls).
Individual tempura pieces start from about 150 yen, and at dinner the house leans into pairing tempura with sparkling wine.

gf_cross_contamination.text: All tempura is fried in wheat-flour batter in shared oil; vegetable pieces share the same fryer as seafood and chicken, so cross-contamination with gluten (and seafood) is inherent.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tempura is accompanied by dipping sauce/soy-based seasonings that conventionally contain wheat; no wheat-free alternatives are indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegetable tempura is fried in the same oil as shrimp, squid, fish, and chicken, and sets are served with fish-based broth and pickles, so plant items are not free of animal cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, modern tempura spot where solo diners are welcome at the partitioned counter; basic Japanese greetings will go a long way, though the simple point-and-order teishoku format makes it manageable even with limited language.

hiro_dashi_to_oden_waiku.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination. Oden simmers in a shared dashi seasoned with soy-sauce-based broth (Japanese soy sauce typically contains wheat), and the menu leans on sashimi with soy sauce, grilled anago, and fried (battered) local chicken. No gluten-free menu or accommodations are documented.
hiro_dashi_to_oden_waiku.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The house dashi is built on bonito (fish) and chicken bone alongside kelp and shiitake, and the core offerings are oden simmered in that stock, fresh seafood sashimi, grilled conger eel, and chicken. No documented vegan dishes.
hiro_dashi_to_oden_waiku.notes: [Mom & Pop] Waiku is a small owner-run oden izakaya tucked on the second floor of a building in Fukuro-cho, just off Namiki-dori in central Hiroshima. It opened in 2016 and has built its identity around carefully made oden served alongside local seafood and sake.

chef_bio.origin: Central Hiroshima (Naka-ku), Seto Inland Sea region
chef_bio.background: Waiku is a small owner-run oden izakaya tucked on the second floor of the Takada Building in Fukuro-cho, just off Namiki-dori in central Hiroshima. It opened in 2016 and has built its identity around carefully made oden served alongside local seafood and sake.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name and spirit center on 'wa' (和) — harmony and human connection — with the owner stating a goal of nurturing a warm space where people bond over a shared meal. The kitchen refuses to cut corners on time or ingredients, building the signature broth from multiple stocks rather than one.
chef_bio.specialty: Oden simmered in a layered house dashi, plus fresh Seto Inland Sea sashimi, grilled conger eel (anago), and karaage of local Hiroshima red chicken, paired with curated Japanese sake.

anecdotes.text: Rather than a single base, the broth is built by combining several dashi sources — bonito, kelp, chicken bone, and shiitake — a layered approach the owner treats as foundational to the oden.
Beyond oden, the kitchen leans on regional character: sashimi from the Seto Inland Sea, grilled conger eel, and karaage made from local Hiroshima red chicken, plus house-made yuzu kosho and miso.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official site states the shop cultivates '人と人との繋がり、すなわち和' (human connection, i.e. 'wa') and builds its dashi by layering 鰹・昆布・鶏ガラ・シイタケ; it lists Seto Inland Sea sashimi, grilled anago, Hiroshima red-chicken karaage and house yuzu kosho/miso. A Tabelog reviewer notes 2016年開業 (opened 2016).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Oden is simmered in a single shared dashi pot seasoned with soy-sauce-based broth, so items share the same wheat-containing liquid.
gf_cross_contamination.source_wording: 「丁寧にうま味を引き出した出汁で炊き上げるおでん。一つ一つ個性の違う食材だからこそ、下ごしらえはより丁寧に。個性の強い揚げ物は全て手作りし、そして湯通ししております。丁寧に丁寧に出汁を回しかけ、じっくりと時間をかけて美味しいおでんに育てるのがわいくの「おでん」です。」(/sp/oden.html)

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The cuisine relies on dashi and soy-sauce seasoning typical of Japanese oden and sashimi; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. No wheat-free soy sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The house dashi is made with bonito (fish) and chicken bone in addition to kelp and shiitake, so even vegetable oden items are cooked in an animal-based stock.

cultural_comfort.note: A cozy local oden counter where a little Japanese helps; staff are welcoming but the experience is geared to Japanese-speaking diners, so a translation app and pointing at the oden pot go a long way.

hiro_menba_jintoku.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. Tsukemen uses wheat noodles and a fish/pork-bone dipping broth with wheat-based soy sauce. A low-carb/konjac noodle option exists for dieters, but the broth and tare are not gluten-free, and there is no documented gluten-free preparation or dedicated equipment.
hiro_menba_jintoku.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The signature broth is a double soup of fish stock and pork bone (tonkotsu), and dishes rely on animal stock and fish powder. No vegan or vegetarian options are documented.
hiro_menba_jintoku.hours_raw: 7:00 PM–4:00 AM (last order 3:30 AM). Closed Sun.
hiro_menba_jintoku.notes: [Mom & Pop] A specialty shop for Kanto-style seafood dipping noodles tucked into Hiroshima's Nagarekawa nightlife quarter, open from evening into the small hours for a late-night bowl.

chef_bio.background: A specialty shop for Kanto-style seafood dipping noodles tucked into Hiroshima's Nagarekawa nightlife quarter, open from evening into the small hours (roughly 7pm to 4am) for a late-night bowl.
chef_bio.philosophy: Guests can dial the spice of the dipping sauce across five levels, and low-carb or konjac noodles are offered for diet-conscious diners.
chef_bio.specialty: House-made medium-thick noodles served with a double broth of fish stock and pork bone (gyokai-tonkotsu), eaten dip-style; the kitchen also makes a spicy mazesoba dusted with fish powder.

anecdotes.text: Diners can choose the spiciness of the dipping sauce from five levels, and lighter low-carb or konjac noodles are available as an alternative.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official site: 神徳特製の中太麺を魚介と豚骨のＷスープで提供 (house medium-thick noodles in a fish + pork-bone double broth), five heat levels, 低糖麺・こんにゃく麺 options, and a 辛まぜそば with fish powder; hours PM7:00-AM4:00 in Nagarekawa, 14 seats, closed Sundays.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat noodles and wheat-based soy sauce are central to the menu, so gluten is present throughout the kitchen; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The dipping broth and tare for tsukemen rely on standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: The soy-sauce attribution is not on the cited page and should be replaced with the seasoning the operator does name — 辛味噌 — which carries its own gluten risk, since 麦味噌 (barley miso) is standard in western Japan; that keeps the field true and better-sourced.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths are made from fish stock and pork bone, and fish powder is used in dishes, so animal products are pervasive.

cultural_comfort.note: A small late-night counter tsukemen shop in the nightlife district where you can order by pointing at the menu, but staff likely speak limited English and it is cash-only, so a little Japanese helps.

hiro_homuraya.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The core dish is tsukemen made with wheat noodles, and the dipping broth uses soy sauce (wheat-based); there is no indication of gluten-free options or accommodation.
hiro_homuraya.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The tsukemen broth is meat/fish-based and the shop's dishes feature pork (chashu/charred pork) and likely fish stock; no vegan options are documented.
hiro_homuraya.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small independent noodle shop in the Higashi-Hakushima area of central Hiroshima, set in a cream-colored multi-story building. It was previously known under the name Mendo Hakushima-ten before becoming Homuraya.

chef_bio.background: A small independent noodle shop on the ground floor of a pale cream-colored three-story building in the Higashi-Hakushima area of central Hiroshima. It was previously known under the name Mendo Hakushima-ten (めん道白島店) before becoming Homuraya.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style tsukemen (spicy dipping noodles), neatly plated and traditionally garnished with lemon; lunch sets pair the noodles with charred-pork rice, and in the evening the shop shifts into an izakaya serving a wider range of dishes.

anecdotes.text: Reviewers describe the tsukemen as having a clean, crisp, refreshing quality with carefully arranged plating, served Hiroshima-style with a wedge of lemon.
The shop is run as a husband-and-wife operation, known locally for generous portions and good value.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog lists it as 焔屋（旧店名 めん道白島店）, 店主さんご夫妻の2名体制 (husband-and-wife 2-person team) in a 淡いクリーム色の3階建て building, praised for ボリュームとコスパ. Syokuki review highlights 整然とした丁寧な盛り付け, Hiroshima-style tsukemen with lemon, charshu-rice lunch sets, and an evening izakaya menu.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The kitchen centers on wheat noodles, so flour and gluten are present throughout; no gluten-free handling is mentioned.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The tsukemen dipping broth uses soy sauce, which in Japan is typically brewed with wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes feature pork (charred pork / chashu) and the broth is meat/fish based, so vegan dishes are not separated or available.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a small, no-frills local noodle shop where ordering in basic Japanese (or by pointing at the menu) will go smoothly, but little to no English is likely, so a foreign student should be comfortable with a casual Japanese-only setting.

hiro_kanseien.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. The core menu—ramen (wheat noodles), gyoza (wheat wrappers), and Chinese dishes seasoned with soy sauce (typically wheat-based)—is built on wheat. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
hiro_kanseien.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The menu centers on meat and seafood dishes (hoikoro/twice-cooked pork, sweet-and-sour pork, ebi chili, char siu, mapo tofu typically made with pork) and uses wheat-based soy sauce. No vegan options are documented.
hiro_kanseien.hours_raw: Mon–Fri 11:00–14:00, 17:00–21:00 (L.O. 20:30); Sat 17:00–21:00 (L.O. 20:30); Sun & holidays closed; occasional irregular closures
hiro_kanseien.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, long-running Chinese restaurant in central Hiroshima's Nobori-cho, a short walk from Hatchobori and the Nagarekawa nightlife district. Founded in 1984, it was renovated and reopened in April 2018, but keeps the feel of a personal, neighborhood eatery with just

chef_bio.background: A small, long-running Chinese restaurant in central Hiroshima's Nobori-cho, a short walk from Hatchobori and the Nagarekawa nightlife district. Founded in 1984, it was renovated and reopened in April 2018, but keeps the feel of a personal, neighborhood eatery with about two dozen seats (24) across a counter and a handful of tables.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen leans on fresh, handmade preparation—favoring domestic ingredients where possible, avoiding frozen products, and cooking with canola oil for a lighter, health-minded finish.
chef_bio.specialty: Home-style Beijing- and Sichuan-leaning Chinese cooking: mapo tofu, twice-cooked pork (hoikoro), sweet-and-sour pork, ebi chili, eight-treasure stir-fry, gyoza, and Chinese-style noodles. A fast, well-priced weekday lunch set is a draw for nearby workers.

anecdotes.text: A regular diner described the lunch mapo tofu as a gentle, mild version with a striking aroma of green onion, served quickly enough to suit the weekday office crowd, with half-portion options that make it easy for solo diners.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official site states 素材はできるだけ国産…冷凍のものは使っておりません and use of canola oil, offering both Beijing and Sichuan cuisine; est. 1984, renovated/reopened April 2018, 24 seats in Nobori-cho near Hatchobori. A blogger describes a mild, green-onion-fragrant lunch mapo tofu served fast with half-portions.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Chinese dishes here are seasoned in the standard way with soy sauce, which is typically wheat-based, and the menu prominently features ramen and gyoza made with wheat.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual neighborhood Chinese spot used to quick lunch-rush regulars; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will get you a friendly, affordable meal, but expect little to no English.

hiro_men_yohaku.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. Ramen noodles are wheat-based, and the soy sauce used in the tare contains wheat. The signature soy and iriko (dried anchovy) broths also rely on these wheat-containing seasonings. No gluten-free options or accommodations are documented.
hiro_men_yohaku.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The broths are built on animal stock (pork, chicken) and iriko dried anchovies, and bowls are topped with pork chashu, chicken, and duck. The side "meat rice" is pork. No vegan or vegetarian options are documented.
hiro_men_yohaku.hours_raw: 11:00-15:00 (often closes earlier when the day's noodles sell out)
hiro_men_yohaku.notes: [Mom & Pop] A tiny nine-seat counter ramen shop tucked into a residential back alley in central Hiroshima, opened in late 2021. Despite its hidden location, it has become one of the most talked-about noodle shops in the city, regularly drawing queues at lunchtime.

chef_bio.background: A tiny nine-seat counter ramen shop tucked into a residential back alley in central Hiroshima (Nishi-Tokaichi-cho), opened on 30 November 2021. Despite its hidden location, it has become one of the most talked-about noodle shops in the city, regularly drawing queues at lunchtime.
chef_bio.specialty: Refined, clear-tasting bowls: a chicken-based soy (shoyu) ramen as the main and an iriko (dried anchovy) ramen as the specialty sub, both with thin, smooth, springy noodles. Bowls can be topped with an assortment of meats — rare and roasted pork chashu, chicken, and duck loin — and a popular side rice bowl topped with meat ('meat rice').

anecdotes.text: Despite being hidden in a quiet alley with no parking (only bike parking), the shop draws lines long enough that it sets out waiting chairs and lets customers preview the posted menu outside while they wait.
It was voted number one in a Hiroshima ramen poll of 176 local fans run by a food blogger, with its premium shoyu bowl (特上醤油) singled out for a restrained, layered, umami-rich broth.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Opening-date site (kaiten-heiten) records a 2021-11-30 open; the owner (trained at Tokyo's らーめんMAIKAGURA and Osaka's 麺一盃) built the shop around a 鶏清湯 shoyu main using 長州黒かしわ鶏 with a sub 瀬戸内いりこ ramen. Modokimaru notes a 9-seat counter, outdoor waiting chairs/menu, no car parking, four meats (rare/hung-roast pork, chicken, duck), and a 176-fan poll that ranked it #1 with the 特上醤油 praised for restrained, layered umami.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The shop's signature bowl is a shoyu (soy sauce) ramen; standard Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, and no wheat-free tare is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Broths and toppings are animal-based (pork, chicken, duck) and use iriko dried anchovies, so there is no separation from animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu is available and dishes are also displayed outside for ordering, so a foreign student can manage easily — just expect to queue and bring cash.

hiro_keirin.gf_detail: This is a traditional Chinese restaurant; dishes rely heavily on wheat-based soy sauce, and items such as fried chicken (唐揚げ), yakisoba, and various stir-fries involve wheat. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented, so it is not suitable for strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_keirin.vegan_detail: The menu centers on meat and seafood (Peking duck, shark-fin soup, seafood yakisoba, fried chicken, ham-and-vegetable sets) and uses wheat soy sauce; while a vegetable stir-fry might be requested, no vegan options are documented and broths/sauces likely contain animal products. Vegans would need to ask carefully in Japanese.
hiro_keirin.notes: A neighborhood Chinese restaurant founded roughly four decades ago, Keirin has become a fixture in central Hiroshima for affordable, generous home-style Chinese cooking. It occupies a multi-floor building with a nostalgic, old-school feel, including plastic food samples

chef_bio.background: A neighborhood Chinese restaurant founded roughly four decades ago, Keirin has become a fixture in central Hiroshima for affordable, generous home-style Chinese cooking. It occupies a multi-floor building with a nostalgic, old-school feel, including plastic food samples lined up in the storefront window and casual triangular tables near the entrance.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen keeps prices reasonable so anyone can enjoy a hearty plate of Chinese home cooking.
chef_bio.specialty: Its signature is the Chinese lunch set (中華ランチ): a single plate piling stir-fried vegetables and protein around a rounded mound of rice, an affectionately described 'grown-up's children's lunch' that keeps regulars coming back. The broader menu ranges from everyday staples like happosai and fried chicken to fuller dishes such as Peking duck, shark-fin soup, and seafood yakisoba.

anecdotes.text: A local food blogger noted that many old-style neighborhood Chinese restaurants have closed over the years, which makes Keirin's enduring, nostalgic 'Chinese lunch' experience all the more cherished by post-war generations.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Syokuki blogger calls the 中華ランチ a 大人のお子様ランチ (happosai, fried chicken, ham, egg over a rice mound on one plate) and laments that 昔ながらの中華屋 are disappearing; the shop is 42年前に創業した. Ekiten's menu lists フカヒレスープ, 海鮮焼きそば and a full 北京ダック; Tabelog shows a multi-floor building with banquet rooms.

gf_cross_contamination.text: As a Chinese kitchen serving fried chicken, noodles, and wheat-soy-sauce dishes, shared fryers and surfaces make cross-contamination very likely; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Chinese dishes here are seasoned with soy sauce, which in Japan is wheat-based.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a longstanding local Chinese restaurant where ordering is in Japanese and English menus are unlikely, but the lunch sets are easy to point to and the casual ground floor is comfortable for solo diners.

hiro_nagarekawa_gyoza_center.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The house specialty is gyoza wrapped in thick wheat-flour skins (the operator is even a gyoza-wrapper maker), and the menu centers on ramen, fried rice and Chinese dishes that rely on wheat-based soy sauce. No gluten-free options or accommodations are documented.
hiro_nagarekawa_gyoza_center.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The signature gyoza are filled with pork, and the menu is built around meat dishes and a green-onion/miso-soy sauce; no vegan or vegetarian dishes are documented.
hiro_nagarekawa_gyoza_center.notes: [Mom & Pop] A downtown gyoza-and-Chinese counter shop that has long been a neighborhood fixture in the Nagarekawa district. When the original elderly owner planned to retire and close, the operators behind the well-known Hiroshima gyoza brand 餃子家 龍 stepped in to keep it alive, reno

chef_bio.origin: Nagarekawa, the nightlife heart of central Hiroshima
chef_bio.background: A downtown gyoza-and-Chinese counter shop that has long been a neighborhood fixture in the Nagarekawa district. When the original elderly owner planned to retire and close, the operators behind the well-known Hiroshima gyoza brand 餃子家 龍 stepped in to keep it alive, renovating the small shop and relaunching it on 20 January 2026 so the local institution would not disappear.
chef_bio.philosophy: Preserve a beloved neighborhood gyoza shop and its thick-skinned, sauce-forward style rather than let it close with its founder.
chef_bio.specialty: Yaki-gyoza with a thick, hand-quality wrapper griddled to a crisp, chewy finish, served with a distinctive green-onion sauce; gyoza also come boiled and in broth, alongside fried rice and other home-style Chinese plates.

anecdotes.text: The shop was set to close when its aging owner prepared to retire, but the company running the 餃子家 龍 gyoza brand took it over, renovated it, and reopened it on 20 January 2026 to carry on the local institution.
The gyoza are described as having a crisp griddled face yet a chewy wrapper, with a naturally sweet filling and a punchy green-onion-based sauce; they are offered fried, boiled, or in broth.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Modokimaru: 店主の高齢により閉店予定だったが、餃子家龍などを展開する会社が事業を引き継ぎ, renovated and reopened 2026-01-20 in Nagarekawa (中区流川町5-27). Menu: 焼き餃子/水餃子/スープ餃子, 炒飯; thick chewy wrappers, naturally sweet filling, chopped green onion + sauce.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The kitchen is built around wheat-skinned gyoza, ramen and fried rice, so flour and wheat-based seasonings are pervasive; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes rely on standard Japanese/Chinese soy-based seasonings, which contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The gyoza are pork-filled and the menu is meat-centered, making cross-contact with animal products unavoidable; no vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny downtown counter-and-table gyoza joint in a nightlife district where ordering in basic Japanese (or pointing at the menu) is expected, so it suits a foreign student comfortable with a little Japanese rather than a full-English experience.

hiro_nihon_ryori_kodama.gf_detail: Traditional Japanese kaiseki built on dashi and soy sauce (typically wheat-based) plus seasonal seafood; no gluten-free program is documented. A gluten-free diner would need to inquire directly in advance, and accommodation is not guaranteed.
hiro_nihon_ryori_kodama.vegan_detail: Omakase courses are centered on Seto Inland Sea seafood (abalone, scallop, mackerel sushi) and fish-based dashi, so the menu is not vegan and there is no documented plant-based option.
hiro_nihon_ryori_kodama.hours_raw: Tue–Fri 17:30–22:00 (L.O. 20:00); Sat–Sun 11:30–14:00 and 17:30–22:00 (L.O. 20:00); closed Monday, year-end/new year, and mid-August.
hiro_nihon_ryori_kodama.notes: [Mom & Pop] Born in the early 1950s in Yamaguchi Prefecture (sources give 1951 or 1952), Kodama was inspired by his father, a former naval cook. chef_bio.background: Born in the early 1950s in Yamaguchi Prefecture (sources give 1951 or 1952), Kodama was inspired by his father, a former naval cook. From age 18 he trained across traditional ryotei, wedding venues, hotels and kappo restaurants, earning the rank of master instructor from the Japan Cooking Association, before opening his own house in 2007.
chef_bio.philosophy: "I want to pay attention to every detail within my reach." Kodama emphasizes drawing out each ingredient's full potential through patient, hand-crafted technique.
chef_bio.specialty: Authentic seasonal Japanese cuisine drawing on Hiroshima's bounty: Seto Inland Sea seafood such as abalone (served with a miso glaze) and scallop, scallop shinjo mousse, saba (mackerel) sushi, and mountain delicacies of the Chugoku region. Served as omakase courses only.

anecdotes.text: His devotion to slow craft is literal: ko-mochi ayu no kanroni (sweetfish simmered with roe) takes two full days of simmering, and kuri no shibukawa-ni (chestnuts cooked in their inner skin) takes three days to complete.
Run warmly by Kodama and his family, the room keeps a homey, family-like atmosphere while holding a crisp, dignified air.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hitosara profiles Kodama Kazuyuki, b.1951 Yamaguchi, inspired by his ex-naval-cook father; trained from age 18 in ryotei, wedding halls, hotels and kappo, holding Japan Cooking Association master-instructor rank; opened his own restaurant in 2007. His 子持ち鮎の甘露煮 simmers a full two days (bones edible) and 栗の渋皮煮 takes three days; omakase includes abalone with miso, scallop shinjo and saba sushi.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Traditional Japanese kaiseki of this style relies on dashi and soy sauce, which is typically wheat-based; no gluten-free preparation is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Courses are built on seafood and fish-based dashi (abalone, scallop, mackerel), so animal products are integral throughout the omakase.

cultural_comfort.note: A refined family-run kaiseki house serving omakase courses only; reservations are essential and you should expect a Japanese-language experience, so a foreign student would do best with some Japanese ability or a Japanese-speaking companion.

hiro_hiranoya.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The signature item is an ice cream monaka, whose wafer shell is made from wheat (and starch), and other listed snacks include a Hiroshima okonomiyaki roll, which is wheat-based. No gluten-free options or allergy accommodations are documented.
hiro_hiranoya.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The headline product is dairy ice cream (vanilla, matcha, chocolate cake, cherry blossom) sandwiched in a monaka wafer, and other items include a meat-wrapped rice ball stick and an okonomiyaki roll. No documented plant-based options.

chef_bio.background: Hiranoya sits right where the crowds spill out of Itsukushima Shrine, about a minute from the shrine exit on Miyajima's approach. It is a family-run souvenir shop that doubles as a tiny rest stop: alongside shelves of straps, magnets, kokeshi dolls, daruma and other Miyajima keepsakes, a small counter with around ten seats serves a few sweet treats to give footsore visitors a place to pause.
chef_bio.specialty: Their signature is the maple-leaf-shaped ice cream monaka (momiji-man ice monaka): a crisp wafer pressed in the shape of Miyajima's famous momiji-manju and filled to order with ice cream, offered in vanilla, matcha, chocolate cake (gato-chocolat) and cherry blossom. They also sell light snacks like a Hiroshima okonomiyaki roll and a meat-wrapped rice ball stick (each around 400 yen).

anecdotes.text: The shop's calling card is a freshly filled ice cream monaka shaped like a momiji (maple leaf), echoing Miyajima's iconic momiji-manju, served as a warm-crisp wafer around cold ice cream.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official site: souvenir shop 厳島神社出口より徒歩1分 with もみじまん・アイスモナカ in バニラ/抹茶/ガトーショコラ/桜 and abundant straps, magnets, kokeshi and daruma. Tabelog confirms ~10 seats inside the souvenir shop and lists 広島お好み焼きロール (¥400) and 肉巻きおにぎり棒 (¥400).

cultural_comfort.note: A casual walk-up souvenir shop and snack counter on the main shrine approach; you can point at the ice cream monaka and a few words of Japanese plus gestures are plenty, though detailed English is not assured.

hiro_tonkatsu_ryori_sachi.gf_detail: This is a tonkatsu specialist: cutlets are coated in wheat flour and panko breadcrumbs and deep-fried, so the core dishes contain gluten. The signature dipping sauce (grated daikon mixed with a secret tare) is also soy-sauce/Worcestershire-style and not gluten-free. No gluten-free menu or accommodations are documented.
hiro_tonkatsu_ryori_sachi.vegan_detail: The entire menu is built around deep-fried pork cutlets (including domestic three-breed pork loin sets). There are no documented vegan or vegetarian main dishes; even sides and the tare sauce are not suitable for vegans.
hiro_tonkatsu_ryori_sachi.notes: Founded in 1975 (Showa 50), Sachi has been frying tonkatsu for local Hiroshima diners for roughly half a century, just west of the Peace Memorial Park in the Sakaimachi neighborhood.

chef_bio.origin: A long-standing independent tonkatsu specialist often cited as part of Hiroshima's tradition of dipping-sauce (tsuke-dare) tonkatsu.
chef_bio.background: Founded in 1975 (Showa 50), Sachi has been frying tonkatsu for local Hiroshima diners for roughly half a century, just west of the Peace Memorial Park in the Sakaimachi neighborhood.
chef_bio.philosophy: Generous, value-focused home-style frying: refillable rice and cabbage, complimentary self-serve coffee at lunch, and a sauce designed to be lighter than typical heavy Worcestershire styles.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is a lighter, refreshing house dipping sauce made by mixing grated daikon radish with a secret tare. The 'Sachi style' is to soak the cutlet in the sauce until the crisp coating just softens before eating. The flagship dish is the Special Loin Cutlet set made with domestic three-breed pork, and rice is the prized Nita-mai from Okuizumo, with free refills of rice and cabbage.

anecdotes.text: Diners describe the 'Sachi style' of dipping the cutlet into the daikon-and-secret-tare sauce until the breading softens, a lighter alternative to heavy sauces.
Rice uses Okuizumo's Nita-mai, called 'the grand champion rice of the west,' and rice and cabbage refills are free.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: mypl (Machipla) article: 昭和50年創業, ~half century of tonkatsu; 秘伝のタレに大根おろし (plus a touch of quail-egg yolk), the 'Sachi style' of soaking the cutlet ヒタヒタ until the breading softens; flagship 国産三元豚 Special Loin set (150g ¥1,600); rice is 西の横綱米 奥出雲の仁多米; free rice/cabbage refills and self-serve lunch coffee.

gf_cross_contamination.text: All cutlets are breaded in wheat flour and panko and deep-fried, so the fryer and core dishes contain gluten; no gluten-free handling is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The house dipping sauce is a secret soy-sauce/Worcestershire-style tare mixed with grated daikon, which typically contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Menu is entirely pork-cutlet based; no vegan or vegetarian options are documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual local tonkatsu shop with no indication of English menus or staff, so a few words of Japanese (and pointing at set-meal photos) will make ordering easiest for a foreign student.

hiro_wafu_kissa_lawn_tonkatsu.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The signature dish is tonkatsu — pork cutlets breaded in wheat-flour batter and panko, then deep-fried. There is no gluten-free menu, and no documented dedicated fryer or allergen accommodation. Side dishes and sauces (tonkatsu sauce) typically contain wheat. Celiac and gluten-sensitive diners should avoid.
hiro_wafu_kissa_lawn_tonkatsu.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. The menu centers on deep-fried pork cutlets (tonkatsu), and sets come with miso soup (commonly fish/dashi based). There are no documented vegan or vegetarian options.
hiro_wafu_kissa_lawn_tonkatsu.hours_raw: 11:00–15:00, 17:30–20:00 (last order applies); closed Sun. Weekday lunch 990 yen. Some sources list evening service until 20:30.
hiro_wafu_kissa_lawn_tonkatsu.notes: The shop opened in 1954 as a Japanese-style café (wafu kissa) and over the decades became beloved by the neighborhood for its tonkatsu, gradually shifting its identity to a tonkatsu specialist while keeping the warm, easygoing café atmosphere.

chef_bio.background: The shop opened in 1954 as a Japanese-style café (wafu kissa) and over the decades became beloved by the neighborhood for its tonkatsu, gradually shifting its identity to a tonkatsu specialist while keeping the warm, easygoing café atmosphere.
chef_bio.philosophy: A focus on quality pork and a lighter fry: cutlets are cooked in rice oil for a crisp, less heavy finish, and lunch sets are generous and affordable with free refills of rice and cabbage plus complimentary coffee.
chef_bio.specialty: Thick-cut pork loin tonkatsu (cutlets over 2cm thick), including premium pork such as Kinka pork (kinkaton) and Ishimi pork loin cutlet sets; weekday lunch specials around 990 yen.

anecdotes.text: Began life in 1954 as a coffee shop before becoming known for its tonkatsu, making it a genuine long-running local institution.
Cutlets are fried in rice oil for a crisp texture with lighter oil; lunch comes with free refills of rice and cabbage and a complimentary coffee.
Known locally for very thick cutlets (over 2cm) and an affordable katsu-sando set, with free parking.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Modokimaru: 1954年に喫茶として開店 then a tonkatsu specialist in Kokutaiji-cho; fried in rice oil, 平日ランチ990円, ご飯とキャベツのおかわり1回無料 plus lunch coffee, using Ishimi pork loin among premium pork. Syokuki: 特厚とんかつ2cm以上, a ~500-yen katsu-sando set, 金華豚, free downtown parking, generous refills.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The core offering is breaded, deep-fried pork (tonkatsu) using wheat batter and panko, so the kitchen and fryer routinely handle gluten; no gluten-free preparation is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: A meat-and-fry focused kitchen with no documented vegan menu; sets include miso soup typically made with fish dashi.

positives.text: Cutlets are fried in rice oil rather than heavier oils, giving a lighter, crisper result (relevant for those avoiding certain oils, though not for gluten or animal-product concerns).

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, longtime local spot where ordering is done by smartphone QR code, so a foreign student with little Japanese can manage, though menus and staff communication are mostly in Japanese.

hiro_nakano_turner_s_hondori_.gf_detail: No gluten-free accommodation is documented. This is a steak and Western/izakaya restaurant; steaks, salt beef and yakiniku are typically seasoned with wheat-based soy sauce and marinades, and the menu also includes okonomiyaki-style Hiroshima dishes whose batter is wheat. No dedicated GF preparation, dedicated fryer, or allergen handling is mentioned on any source. A celiac or strict gluten-free diner should not assume safe options here without direct confirmation in person.
hiro_nakano_turner_s_hondori_.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The restaurant is a meat-focused steakhouse — its signature dishes are steak, house-made salt beef, and yakiniku. No vegan or vegetarian menu or accommodations are documented on any source.
hiro_nakano_turner_s_hondori_.hours_raw: Lunch 12:00–14:00 (L.O. 14:00); Dinner 17:00–00:00 (L.O. 23:30). Open year-round except Dec 31 and Jan 1. (Tabelog listing notes a Wednesday closure and 11:30 lunch start; Hitosara, the more current source, lists open daily with 12:00 lunch start.)

chef_bio.background: Born in 1989 in Hiroshima Prefecture, the head chef and branch manager Sugishima Yasuhiro found his way into cooking through an unexpected door — a part-time job at an okonomiyaki shop. From there he trained formally across several styles, including teppanyaki, traditional Japanese cuisine, and Western cooking, before joining the company behind this restaurant in 2012 and taking over as manager of the Hondori main branch in 2014.
chef_bio.philosophy: He brings together skills cultivated through a deliberately varied culinary background to create the restaurant's hearty, meat-forward dining experience.
chef_bio.specialty: American- and Canadian-style meat cookery — steaks, house-made salt beef, and teppanyaki — drawing on nearly two decades across multiple culinary disciplines.

anecdotes.text: His culinary career began almost by accident, working part-time at an okonomiyaki restaurant before he trained across teppanyaki, Japanese, and Western kitchens.
The house signature is the generous 'Turner's Steak,' served alongside a house-made salt beef, in a multi-level space ranging from an intimate loft to a pet-friendly terrace.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hitosara profile: 杉島保広, b.1989 Hiroshima; got into cooking via an okonomiyaki part-time job, trained in teppanyaki, Japanese and Western cuisine, joined the company in 2012 and became Hondori branch manager in 2014; ~19 years' experience specializing in American/Canadian meat cookery. Restaurant page notes the signature Turner's Steak and house salt beef across a multi-level space.

cultural_comfort.note: A lively, popular central-Hiroshima steakhouse and izakaya where a few words of Japanese will help; staff are used to a casual crowd but English support is not documented, so come ready to point at the menu.

hiro_sobaya_katsuki.gf_detail: The noodles themselves are jūwari (100% buckwheat, no wheat binder), but this is a traditional soba-ya, not a gluten-free kitchen. The dipping tsuyu is made with standard Japanese soy sauce (contains wheat), and the kitchen and water bath handle nothing as gluten-free. No dedicated gluten-free preparation, separate utensils, or wheat-free sauce is documented. Not safe for those requiring strict gluten avoidance.
hiro_sobaya_katsuki.vegan_detail: A traditional soba shop whose tsuyu is built on katsuo/fish-based dashi and soy sauce, and the menu features items such as maki-sushi. No vegan-specific menu or preparation is documented. Not suitable for vegans.
hiro_sobaya_katsuki.hours_raw: 11:00-14:00 / 17:00-21:00 (L.O. 20:30). Dinner service (17:00-21:00) is offered on Monday and Thursday only (excluding holidays). Closed Wednesday. Often sells out and closes early when the day's soba runs out.
hiro_sobaya_katsuki.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, independent soba-ya in the Tōkaichimachi neighborhood of central Hiroshima, west of the Peace Memorial Park. The shop has built a devoted local following and is regularly named among the city's best soba destinations.

chef_bio.background: A small, independent soba-ya in the Tōkaichimachi neighborhood of central Hiroshima, west of the Peace Memorial Park. The shop has built a devoted local following and is regularly named among the city's best soba destinations.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner keeps the dining room deliberately uncrowded, spacing the tables to give each guest a calm, unhurried meal.
chef_bio.specialty: Jūwari soba — noodles made from 100% buckwheat with no wheat binder. Diners choose between 'white' soba (marunuki, from hulled buckwheat for a smoother, more delicate noodle) and 'black' soba (hikigurumi, whole-grain, with a pronounced buckwheat aroma and a firmer, chewier bite). Hand-rolled maki-sushi is a noted side.

anecdotes.text: The noodles are so sought-after that one writer reported being turned away on multiple visits because the shop had already sold out and closed for the day — they pour the day's batch of fresh juwari and stop when it is gone.
Regulars debate white vs black: the whole-grain black soba delivers the fullest buckwheat fragrance and a firm chew, while the white is prized for a smoother finish.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Japanese food blogs (nisinihonwalker, modokimaru) describe a Tokaichimachi jūwari soba shop with ~16-18 generously spaced table seats, black (whole-grain) and white soba, a sell-out/close-when-gone model, and a 3-piece maki-sushi side; owner name not published.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a traditional soba shop, not a gluten-free kitchen; even though the noodles are 100% buckwheat, the dipping sauce uses wheat-containing soy sauce and there is no documented separation for gluten-sensitive diners.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Tsuyu (dipping sauce) is standard Japanese soy-sauce-based, which contains wheat; no wheat-free sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Tsuyu and dashi are fish/katsuo-based and the menu includes maki-sushi, so dishes are not vegan and no plant-based alternatives are documented.

positives.text: Noodles are jūwari (100% buckwheat, no wheat flour binder), so the soba itself contains no wheat — though it is prepared in a kitchen that handles wheat-based sauces.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, popular local soba shop with no English menu noted — a little basic Japanese (or pointing at the white vs black soba) helps, and arrive early since they close once the day's noodles sell out.

hiro_dashi_to_soba_suisha.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The noodles are described as smooth Sarashina-style soba, which mixes buckwheat with wheat flour, and tempura uses a wheat batter. The standard dashi is also made with bonito and finished with soy sauce (which contains wheat). There is no documented gluten-free menu, no dedicated noodle pot, and no allergen protocol published. Celiac travelers should avoid.
hiro_dashi_to_soba_suisha.vegan_detail: Has a genuine, dedicated plant-based menu line ("プラントベース"/vegan zaru soba) using an animal-free dashi made from kombu, shiitake mushrooms and vegetables instead of the regular bonito-based broth — staff-developed specifically so guests who do not eat animal products (and Muslim/halal-conscious diners) can eat here. Note the standard menu (oyster soba, tempura soba, most warm-broth dishes) uses bonito/fish dashi and is not vegan, so order specifically from the plant-based items. The vegan offering is broth-and-noodles; the noodles themselves still contain wheat, so it is vegan-friendly but not gluten-free.
hiro_dashi_to_soba_suisha.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun, holidays, days before holidays, and days after holidays 11:00 - 21:30 (closures follow Ekie's schedule)

chef_bio.background: Suisha is run by the Hiroshima food company 三吉屋食品株式会社. The original 'Suisha' soba house opened in the Aqua Hiroshima Center-gai arcade on October 18, 1995, and this Hiroshima Station branch inside ekie opened on March 29, 2018, later refreshed into its current 'DASHI to SOBA' concept with new lattice woodwork by a local carpenter.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's stated motto is 気軽に気楽に気兼ねなく — to be enjoyed 'casually, comfortably, without holding back' — positioning it as an approachable, family-friendly soba stop at the station.
chef_bio.specialty: Dashi-forward soba: the kitchen grinds and brews its broth fresh each morning, working with eight distinct stocks (kombu dashi, white dashi, soba dashi, joujiru, soba-gaeshi, don-gaeshi, don dashi and tempura-don dashi). The base first-press dashi blends three kinds of bonito shavings from waters off Kumamoto and Nagasaki with Rishiri kombu from Hokkaido, finished in a slightly sweet Kansai style the shop notes is unusual for Hiroshima. The smooth Sarashina-style noodles are paired with tempura, and signature plates include ten-zaru soba, a refreshing Setouchi lemon soba, and an evening sake-and-soba 'banshaku' set.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen developed an animal-free plant-based dashi (kombu, shiitake and vegetables) so that guests who avoid animal products and Muslim/halal-conscious travelers can enjoy the same soba; the plant-based zaru soba is offered at both the ekie and the Aqua Center-gai branches.
The shop's plant-based soba has been featured in an English-language vegetarian guidebook published by the Chugoku Economic Federation.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's own site (fusha-suisha.net) and its ekie page confirm operation by 三吉屋食品, the 1995 Aqua Center-gai and 2018 ekie openings, the 気軽に気楽に気兼ねなく motto, eight house stocks, a slightly sweet Kansai-style first dashi (Kumamoto/Nagasaki katsuo + Rishiri kombu), Sarashina noodles, and a kombu-shiitake-vegetable plant-based dashi for vegan/halal guests featured in a Chugoku Economic Federation vegetarian guidebook.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Sarashina-style soba noodles are made from buckwheat blended with wheat flour and are boiled in shared water; no gluten-free noodle or dedicated pot is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The regular dashi/tare is finished with soy sauce and the kitchen runs multiple soy-based stocks (soba-gaeshi, don-gaeshi, etc.); standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The plant-based dashi is animal-free, but it is prepared in the same kitchen that runs bonito-based broths and shared noodle-boiling water; no separate-equipment or cross-contact protocol is published.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Only general guidance is given: bringing homemade food for infants/preschoolers with allergies is allowed with prior consultation; no allergen chart or formal allergy-handling protocol is published.

positives.text: Offers a dedicated, staff-developed plant-based (vegan) soba using a kombu-shiitake-vegetable dashi with no animal ingredients, explicitly aimed at guests who cannot eat animal products and at international visitors.
The plant-based menu is described as halal-conscious ('ハラール対応'), though no formal halal certification is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, walk-in noodle shop right inside Hiroshima Station with picture-friendly menus and a relaxed "come as you are" attitude; a foreign student can comfortably point-and-order, though staff communication will mostly be in Japanese.

hiro_asahi_coffee_salon_ebisu.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering. This is a traditional coffeehouse whose food centers on toast, sandwiches, cakes and omelet-curry — all wheat-based. No dedicated GF menu or cross-contamination handling is documented.
hiro_asahi_coffee_salon_ebisu.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly destination. Morning sets and dishes feature eggs, dairy, natto with dried shrimp, and cakes; no documented vegan options. Black coffee is the only reliably plant-based item.
