chef_bio.background: Asahi Coffee Salon was founded in 1950 by the company that still runs it (朝日コーヒーショップ), and this Ebisucho branch opened in 1968 in the basement of a building beneath the bustling Ebisu shopping street in central Hiroshima. Stepping down from the busy street, guests find a hushed, Showa-era interior that has kept its vintage character for decades, complete with antique touches.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop operates under the spirit of "心贈ります" (offering heart/sincerity), aiming to give each guest thoughtful service and a sense of calm, and on serving nutritionally balanced morning meals to energize locals.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-drip original-blend coffee with a deep, easy-drinking flavor, served alongside generous morning sets, cakes, and retro café fare such as omelet curry.

anecdotes.text: All the tables and chairs are handcrafted in a traditional style meant to help guests relax, and the calm Showa atmosphere stands in deliberate contrast to the busy street above.
A signature "Health Set" morning (750 yen) tops toast with shiso leaf and natto mixed with dried shrimp and green onion, reflecting the shop's focus on nourishing breakfasts.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site and Tabelog confirm a 1950 company founding, the 1968 basement branch in Horikawa-cho/Ebisu near the Hatchobori stop, the 心贈ります motto, custom-made tables and chairs, hand-drip original blend, omelet curry, and a 750-yen shiso-and-natto Health Set morning.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed Showa-era basement coffeehouse where a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will get you through; little English is expected, but the calm atmosphere and simple coffee-and-toast offerings make it easy for a foreign student.

hiro_kissa_mekuru.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering is documented. This is a toast-and-baked-goods kissaten — morning sets center on wheat toast and French toast, and the signature item is a flour-adjacent pudding; bread is the core of the menu, so it is not suitable for strict gluten avoidance.
hiro_kissa_mekuru.vegan_detail: Not a vegan place. The menu is built around toast with butter, boiled eggs, yogurt, bacon/scrambled eggs, and pudding (egg/dairy), so most morning and cafe items contain dairy and egg. A plain black coffee or tea works, and one might ask about toast without butter, but there is no documented vegan menu.

One review blog lists morning 08:30–10:30 then 11:00–16:00, closed Sundays/holidays plus irregular closures. An older cafe blog lists 08:00–18:00 closed Wednesday. The Sunday-closed, early-afternoon-close pattern appears in the more recent sources.

chef_bio.background: A small, much-loved neighborhood coffee shop in Tokaichimachi, a short walk west of the Peace Memorial Park, opened in February 2012 and run by its owner with a small staff. The interior was renovated with bare concrete floors and plaster walls, then warmed with dried flowers hung from the ceiling, wicker baskets, postcards, and vintage school-style chairs, giving it a nostalgic, cozy feel.
chef_bio.philosophy: A calm, healing space meant to let visitors slow down and relax over a simple, carefully made breakfast.
chef_bio.specialty: Morning sets served until early afternoon: thick buttered toast (including a butter-cinnamon-sugar version) or French toast with a boiled egg, thick homemade-style yogurt, and a small vegetable soup, presented on aluminum trays that evoke a school lunch. The firm-set house pudding (めくるプリン) with bitter caramel is a signature.

anecdotes.text: The name めくる means 'to turn pages,' echoed by a small library of books in the shop for customers to leaf through.
Simple-looking plates show real care: the yogurt is thick and creamy and the vegetable soup is described as having flavor seeped all the way through.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Kotogurashi, modokimaru and Tabelog confirm a Tokaichimachi kissaten opened February 10, 2012, run by the owner with one staff member (~20 seats), a renovated bare-concrete/plaster interior with school chairs and dried flowers, aluminum-tray morning sets with cinnamon-sugar toast, the 'to turn pages' name with in-shop books, and the firm めくるプリン with bitter caramel.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, homey neighborhood coffee shop run by the owner and one or two staff; little to no English is documented, so a few words of Japanese and a relaxed, polite approach will make ordering the morning set easy.

hiro_t_s_cafe_gate_in.gf_detail: No gluten-free offerings documented. As a traditional kissaten serving parfaits, cakes, toast, sandwiches, pasta, and rice-plate lunches, wheat is present throughout the menu (bread, pastries, parfait components, batters). No dedicated gluten-free preparation or labeling is mentioned anywhere.
hiro_t_s_cafe_gate_in.vegan_detail: Not a vegan-friendly destination. The signature draw is fresh-milk soft-serve parfaits, and the lunch bento centers on meat dishes; coffee-shop fare relies on dairy and eggs. No vegan menu or plant-based options are documented.

chef_bio.background: Gate In is a retro kissaten (classic Japanese coffee house) that opened in 1976 in the Otemachi district of central Hiroshima, just steps from the Kamiyacho-nishi tram stop and within easy walking distance of Peace Memorial Park and the A-Bomb Dome. For roughly half a century it has held its prime corner near the Edion twin towers, keeping the calm, settled atmosphere of an old-school cafe.
chef_bio.philosophy: A long-running local gathering spot that has quietly watched over the neighborhood and its children for decades.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal fresh-fruit parfaits built on house fresh-milk soft-serve ice cream, with rotating offerings such as fig and Earl Grey, Shine Muscat, and Hiroshima-lemon parfaits; also known for daily made-to-order lunch bento.

anecdotes.text: A decorative white horse holding a cup stands at the entrance as the shop's landmark. Inside it hides an encouraging message that children can only read once they have grown tall enough to peer in - 'You've grown up' - a small token of the cafe watching over neighborhood kids as they grow.
The cafe is famous locally for its photogenic seasonal parfaits made with premium fruit like Shine Muscat and Hiroshima lemon over smooth fresh-milk soft serve, drawing a steady following.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Pecomag and Tabelog confirm a 1976 Otemachi kissaten near the Kamiyacho-nishi tram, the white-horse landmark with a hidden 'you've grown up' message readable only once children grow tall enough, seasonal fresh-milk soft-serve fruit parfaits (fig/Earl Grey, Shine Muscat, Hiroshima lemon), and made-to-order lunch bento.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed, classic neighborhood coffee house where a foreign student can comfortably point at the parfait menu and get by with a few Japanese greetings; English support is not advertised.

There is no gluten-free menu or documented gluten-free accommodation. The only naturally gluten-free items are the fresh-pressed seasonal fruit juices and coffee/tea.

chef_bio.background: Furufuru is a long-running retro coffeehouse tucked just off Namiki-dori in central Hiroshima's Mikawacho, on the ground floor of a distinctive red-brick building marked by a blue-and-white striped awning at the door. It opened in 1973 (Shōwa 48) and has been pouring coffee here for around half a century.
chef_bio.specialty: Morning sets and freshly made sandwiches, plus seasonal fresh-pressed single-fruit juices that rotate through strawberry, golden kiwi, plum, grape, peach, and pear, and a beloved house-made pudding crowned with whipped cream.

anecdotes.text: The small room is wrapped in a vintage European mood: every window is set with stained glass, the walls wear fabric-like patterned wallpaper, and soft jazz keeps the air calm and unhurried.
Doors open at 9 a.m. with an affordable morning set served until 11, pairing a little fruit with toast, sandwiches, or a grilled sandwich and coffee or tea.
The house-made pudding is a signature: smooth and gently sweet under a generous cap of whipped cream.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog gives a 1973 (Shōwa 48) opening for an 18-seat Mikawacho kissaten; tabetainjya describes the red-brick building with a blue-and-white striped awning, all-stained-glass windows, jazz, a 9-11am morning set, rotating single-fruit fresh juices (strawberry, golden kiwi, plum, grape, peach, La France pear), and a house pudding under whipped cream. Owner name not published.

positives.text: Seasonal fresh-pressed single-fruit juices are available, which are naturally plant-based and gluten-free, though preparation handling is not documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, old-school neighborhood coffeehouse where no English is expected and the menu is in Japanese, so a foreign student should come prepared to point at items or use a translation app and follow the quiet, relaxed pace of the room.

hiro_bora_bora_tatemachi.gf_detail: This is a traditional Showa-era coffee house whose food menu is built on toast, sandwiches, hotcakes and similar light fare — all wheat-based. There is no documented gluten-free preparation, no dedicated equipment, and no indication of GF awareness. Not a viable option for those who must strictly avoid gluten; at most one could order a black coffee or cream soda.
hiro_bora_bora_tatemachi.vegan_detail: The menu centers on egg, cheese and ham toast, hotcakes and house-made dressing — egg- and dairy-heavy with no documented vegan dishes. Black coffee and cream soda (syrup + soda) may be incidentally plant-based, but there is no stated vegan offering or accommodation. Not a vegan destination.
hiro_bora_bora_tatemachi.hours_raw: Mon–Fri 07:00–19:30; Sat 07:00–17:30; Sun & holidays 08:00–17:30. Morning service 07:00–11:00 (Sun/holidays 08:00–11:00). (Some sources list closing as 19:00/17:00; Tabelog lists 19:30/17:30.)

chef_bio.background: Bora Bora opened in 1976 and has remained a fixture of central Hiroshima's coffee-house culture for nearly half a century. The 'Tatemachi branch' name dates from a time when the shop had more than one location. Tucked along a lane off Hondori near the Tatemachi tram stop, it keeps the unhurried Showa-era spirit alive, opening early at 7 a.m. for the morning crowd.
chef_bio.philosophy: A classic 'junkissa' approach: quality coffee, simple light fare, and a calm, nostalgic room where regulars can linger over a newspaper.
chef_bio.specialty: Morning toast sets (plain, cheese, or ham toast with salad and coffee), plus longtime favorites like hotcakes and a vivid cream soda. The house-made salad dressing became so popular with regulars that the shop began bottling and selling it separately.

anecdotes.text: Step inside and you find a brick-walled interior you would never guess from the street, with a striking blue-tiled roof feature carried indoors, green-tiled table seating and matching lamps, and a small kamidana (household shrine) high on the wall.
The house dressing proved so popular that regulars' demand led the shop to sell it in bottles to take home.
The morning fare is light and unfussy — toast sets, hotcakes and a bright cream soda — true to a traditional coffee house, served from 7 a.m. in a coffee-scented, relaxing room.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Junkissa.blog, morning-hiroshima and modokimaru confirm a 1976 founding, the 立町店 name as a remnant of former multiple locations, a brick interior with blue-tile roof feature, green-tile seating, matching lamps and a kamidana, a 7am opening, plain/cheese/ham toast sets, hotcakes and cream soda, and a house salad dressing sold in bottles by customer demand.

cultural_comfort.note: A welcoming neighborhood retro café where a foreign student can comfortably order a simple morning set or coffee, but the staff are an older couple and menus/conversation are in Japanese, so a little preparation or a translation app helps.

hiro_koryoriya_nagayama.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The kitchen runs on Japanese soy sauce (wheat-based) and the miso soups and seasoned side dishes use soy-sauce/miso preparations; some onigiri fillings (shrimp tempura, corn tempura) are battered in wheat, and the menu rotates without published allergen handling. No gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or allergen accommodation is documented. Plain salt onigiri and umeboshi (pickled plum) onigiri with nori are inherently low-gluten items, but cross-contamination from a shared kitchen cannot be ruled out — a celiac traveler should not rely on this place.
hiro_koryoriya_nagayama.vegan_detail: Not vegan or vegetarian. The house dashi is made from bonito (katsuobushi), tuna, and kombu, so even vegetable-forward miso soups and side dishes contain fish stock. Miso soup varieties include pork (tonjiru-style) broths, and popular onigiri fillings are grilled mackerel, mentaiko (pollock roe), and seasoned ground meat. While the menu emphasizes fresh vegetables, there is no documented animal-free preparation, so it does not suit vegan or strict vegetarian diners.
hiro_koryoriya_nagayama.hours_raw: Sat morning 7:30-10:00; Lunch Mon-Sat 10:00-14:30 (L.O. 14:00); Dinner Wed-Thu 18:00-21:00, Fri-Sat 18:00-22:00. Closed Sundays (and Mondays that fall on national holidays). Note: hours vary somewhat across listings; the official site shows no Mon/Tue dinner service.

chef_bio.background: An intimate roughly-15-seat washoku spot run by owner-chef Ryunosuke Nagayama. It began life as an evening izakaya, but during the COVID-19 pandemic the owner started serving morning and lunch sets, and the daytime onigiri-and-miso-soup teishoku grew so popular that lines now form regularly.
chef_bio.philosophy: The chef cooks around peak-season produce, noting that an ingredient's true peak is fleeting, and keeps seasoning simple and refined to draw out vegetable umami. The house dashi is built carefully from bonito, tuna (maguro-bushi), and kombu, and the kitchen leans into the benefits of fermented foods like miso.
chef_bio.specialty: An onigiri-and-miso-soup teishoku lunch: diners choose an onigiri (salt, umeboshi, mentaiko, grilled mackerel, shrimp or corn tempura, seasonal mushroom, or seasoned meat) and a miso soup (pork tonjiru-style, seasonal vegetable, and rotating creations), served with about five small vegetable-forward side dishes; additional onigiri can be added.

anecdotes.text: The lunch service was born out of the pandemic pivot: the formerly evening-only izakaya added morning and lunch sets and became a queue-forming local favorite.
The owner sources produce that does not appear in supermarkets, such as premium Hokkaido tomatoes, and builds custom broth ratios for each day's miso soup.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The shop's site plus pecomag and tabiiro confirm owner-chef 永山龍之助, ~14-15 seats, an evening izakaya that added COVID-era morning/lunch service now drawing queues, an onigiri (salt, umeboshi, mentaiko, grilled mackerel, shrimp/corn tempura, mushroom, seasoned meat) and miso-soup teishoku with five side dishes and a bonito/tuna/kombu dashi, plus produce such as premium Hokkaido tomatoes not sold in supermarkets. Extra onigiri are addable (for an extra charge).

gf_cross_contamination.text: Shared home-style kitchen with wheat-based soy sauce, miso preparations, and battered tempura onigiri fillings; no gluten-free protocol is documented, so cross-contamination should be assumed.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Side dishes and seasonings use Japanese soy sauce (standard shoyu is wheat-based), e.g. blanched bitter melon dressed in ponzu.

vegan_cross_contact.text: House dashi is made from bonito, tuna, and kombu, so vegetable miso soups and side dishes still contain fish stock; some miso soups also include pork.

positives.text: Menu emphasizes fresh seasonal vegetables and several side dishes, and plain salt or umeboshi onigiri with nori are simple options, though none are prepared as certified allergen-free.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a tiny, locals-favorite counter spot where staff likely speak mostly Japanese and lunch queues form, so a few basic Japanese phrases and patience go a long way for a foreign student.

hiro_peace_blvd.gf_detail: The core appeal is rice (onigiri), which is naturally gluten-free, and the prized Okuizumo Nita-mai (仁多米) is the centerpiece. However, sets are built around Japanese sides and dishes that commonly use wheat-containing soy sauce and miso, and listed mains such as fried oysters (kaki-fry) and grilled anago use wheat batter/sauce. No gluten-free protocol, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling is documented, so a strictly gluten-free diner would need to ask in detail and verify each component.
hiro_peace_blvd.vegan_detail: Set meals are centered on fish and meat (e.g., simmered mackerel/saba, fried oysters, grilled anago) and use dashi/miso/soy-based seasonings, so the standard offerings are not vegan. Plain salted onigiri rice and some vegetable sides (e.g., spinach with white-miso dressing) may be plant-forward, but no vegan menu, vegan dashi, or animal-free preparation is documented; a vegan diner would need to ask whether any plant-only combination can be assembled.
hiro_peace_blvd.hours_raw: Weekdays (Mon-Fri): 11:00-14:00 (L.O. 13:30); Sat/Sun/holidays: 10:00-17:00 (L.O. 16:30). Note: at the time of one report the cafe was operating shortened hours; normal hours were expected to run later.
hiro_peace_blvd.notes: [Mom & Pop] Peace Blvd opened on June 1, 2020 as an onigiri cafe attached to the flagship shop of Nitaya, a Hiroshima onigiri specialist. The building's ground floor pairs two storefronts: the takeout-only Onigiri Nitaya Otemachi main shop on one side and the eat-in Peace Blvd on t

chef_bio.origin: Hiroshima (Otemachi, Naka-ku); the rice comes from Okuizumo in Shimane.
chef_bio.background: Peace Blvd opened on June 1, 2020 as an onigiri cafe attached to the flagship shop of Nitaya, a Hiroshima onigiri specialist. The building's ground floor pairs two storefronts: the takeout-only Onigiri Nitaya Otemachi main shop on one side and the eat-in Peace Blvd on the other, where the same rice balls are served as proper sit-down set meals. The name nods to the shop's location near Peace Memorial Park and Peace Boulevard.
chef_bio.philosophy: Let the rice be the star: the onigiri are salted to highlight the rice's natural sweetness, with the quality of the Nita-mai itself treated as the main attraction rather than elaborate fillings.
chef_bio.specialty: Onigiri set meals built on prized Okuizumo Nita-mai rice, served as a daily-changing lunch with a main, sides and miso soup; the shop also offers a fuller Nitaya onigiri zen, plus sweets such as parfaits and fondant chocolat.

anecdotes.text: Reviewers single out the rice itself as the real draw, describing the salting as balanced to bring out the rice's sweetness and the rice as genuinely delicious.
The eat-in cafe sits beside the takeout-only Nitaya Otemachi main shop, which supplies its onigiri and bento, letting visitors near Peace Park enjoy the same rice balls as a relaxed set meal.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabetainjya and modokimaru confirm Peace Blvd opened June 1, 2020 as the eat-in counterpart to the takeout-only Onigiri Nitaya Otemachi main shop, serving set meals built on Okuizumo Nita-mai rice salted to highlight its sweetness, plus a Nitaya onigiri zen and sweets like parfaits and fondant chocolat.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Set meals feature Japanese dishes such as simmered mackerel and white-miso-dressed vegetables, which in standard Japanese cooking use soy sauce and miso that typically contain wheat; no wheat-free seasoning is documented.

positives.text: The cafe centers on rice and onigiri made from high-grade Okuizumo Nita-mai, and plain salted rice balls are naturally gluten-free even though the surrounding set components are not.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, welcoming onigiri set-meal spot a short walk from the Peace Park where a few words of Japanese and pointing at the daily lunch will get you a friendly, easy meal; solo diners are comfortable at the counter.

hiro_mon_hatchobori_ten.gf_detail: This is a wheat-bread bakery; the signature gratin rings, curry rings, sandwiches, croissants and loaves are all made from wheat flour, so there are no gluten-free options. No gluten-free products or accommodations are documented.
hiro_mon_hatchobori_ten.vegan_detail: The menu centers on bread and cafe dishes using dairy, eggs and meat — the house specialties are a gratin ring (cream/cheese roux) and curry ring, plus hot sandwiches, omelette rice, doria and parfaits. No vegan options are documented.

hiro_mon_hatchobori_ten.notes: [Mom & Pop] MON is a long-established Hiroshima bakery founded in 1953 (described as a roughly 65-year-old shop). From its earliest days it has baked bread in a French stone-bed (stone-floor) oven, aiming for a crisp crust and a moist, tender crumb.

chef_bio.background: MON is a long-established Hiroshima bakery founded in 1953 (described as a roughly 65-year-old shop). From its earliest days it has baked bread in a French stone-bed (stone-floor) oven, aiming for a crisp crust and a moist, tender crumb.
chef_bio.philosophy: The bakery wants its bread to be eaten as a staple in place of rice, so it puts particular care into its loaf breads, choosing select ingredients and baking slowly over time.
chef_bio.specialty: Its signature item is the gratin ring (a ring-shaped bread filled with house-made roux); the curry ring and curry doughnut are also popular, and all the roux fillings are made in-house. At the Hatchobori branch, bread is baked at the main Minamitakeya location and delivered within about 15 minutes, offering 30-40 varieties daily.

anecdotes.text: The Hatchobori branch was designed with a softer white-and-pink interior and offers pasta lunch sets and omelette rice not available at the main shop, aimed at welcoming female customers.
The shop has used a French stone-bed oven since its founding to give the bread a crisp exterior and moist interior.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: MON's official site and Tabelog confirm a 1953 (Shōwa 28) founding, a French stone-bed oven used since founding for a crisp-crust/moist-crumb loaf, a bread-as-staple philosophy, the signature gratin ring with house-made roux (plus curry ring and curry doughnut), and a Hatchobori branch with a white-and-pink interior, pasta/omelette-rice lunches, and 30-40 daily varieties baked at the Minamitakeya main shop and delivered within ~15 minutes.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, cash-only neighborhood bakery-cafe with no indication of English support, so a foreign student would do best with a translation app or a Japanese-speaking friend to navigate the menu.

hiro_yoshizushi.gf_detail: Edomae sushi here is finished with wheat-based soy sauce (nikiri) and uses cooked/cured fish; no gluten-free program is documented. Not suitable for strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_yoshizushi.vegan_detail: An omakase sushi counter built around fish and seafood, with wheat-soy seasonings throughout. No vegan offering is documented.

chef_bio.background: A Hiroshima native who fell for cooking as a child and discovered sushi during his university years, Yoshimura trained in Tokyo to learn the techniques and discipline of Edomae sushi before returning home. He opened his own counter at age 35 and has run it for decades.
chef_bio.philosophy: He works by the motto 'opening for the first time today' (本日開店) — approaching each day's service with fresh sincerity, aiming for craftsmanship and hospitality that leave a lasting impression on guests.
chef_bio.specialty: Edomae sushi using seasonal fish from the Seto Inland Sea and the Sea of Japan, prepared with classic techniques of curing (shime), marinating (zuke), and aging (nekasu). The rice is seasoned with red vinegar and salt rather than sugar, to draw out its natural sweetness and umami.

anecdotes.text: Ingredients are chosen by the chef himself, with the day's fish selected fresh before service.
Yoshimura opened the restaurant at age 35 after his Tokyo apprenticeship and has built it into one of the region's most respected sushi counters.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hitosara and the shop's gorp site confirm chef 吉村憲治, a Hiroshima native who discovered sushi at university, trained in Tokyo, opened his own counter at 35, the 本日開店 motto, a 9-10-seat counter, shari seasoned with only salt and red vinegar (no sugar), seasonal Seto Inland Sea/Sea of Japan fish, and 〆る・漬ける・ねかせる (curing/marinating/aging) techniques.

cultural_comfort.note: This is an intimate, higher-end omakase sushi counter where the chef sets the pace; some Japanese-language ability and reservation etiquette help, and it suits a special occasion rather than a casual drop-in.

hiro_kanayama_base.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering documented. The signature dishes are breaded-and-fried katsu sandwiches (wheat bread and wheat-flour coating) and sandwiches generally, so the core menu is wheat-based. Sauces likely use standard wheat-containing soy sauce. Treat as not suitable for celiac/gluten-free diners.
hiro_kanayama_base.vegan_detail: No vegan options documented. The menu centers on meat (steak plates, pork-cutlet katsu sandwiches) and a coffee/bar lineup; nothing on the page indicates plant-based dishes. Not a vegan-friendly destination.
hiro_kanayama_base.hours_raw: Mon-Wed, Fri-Sun 08:00-22:00; Thursday closed. (One local write-up notes hours can be irregular.)
hiro_kanayama_base.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, casual American-style cafe and bar tucked into the Ginzan-cho neighborhood of central Hiroshima, an easy walk from the Hatchobori area and within the Peace Memorial Park orbit. chef_bio.background: A small, casual American-style cafe and bar in the Ginzan-cho (銀山町) neighborhood of central Hiroshima's Naka-ku, an easy walk from the Hatchobori area. It sits right by the Ginzancho tram stop, with the Kyobashi River just to the east, in a low-key local pocket rather than a tourist strip.
chef_bio.specialty: Hearty, value-minded plates with an American-casual feel: katsu sandwiches and other sandwiches, and a popular one-plate steak-and-rice lunch for around 1,000 yen, plus coffee and a bar menu. The shop opens early (from 8am), so morning service is offered too.

anecdotes.text: Locals point out the shop name 銀山 is read 'Kanayama' (not 'Kinzan' or 'Kanakin'), a quirk noted for visitors from outside the prefecture.
Known for offering a satisfying 'stamina' steak lunch for around 1,000 yen, served as a steak-and-rice plate.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Syokuki confirms the name is read 'Kanayama' (not Kinzan/Kanakin), the Ginzancho/Naka-ku (中区銀山町1-2) location, the American-casual cafe-and-bar concept, 8:00–21:00 hours and the sub-¥1,000 steak lunch. Owner name is not published.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed neighborhood cafe-bar where a friendly greeting and pointing at the menu will get you by; some basic Japanese helps as it is a small local spot rather than a tourist-facing place.

hiro_shizenshoku_restaurant_k.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented. As a Japanese natural-food kitchen, seasonings such as miso and soy sauce typically contain wheat, and items like the lemon cake are wheat-based. There is no stated dedicated fryer or allergen protocol, so a celiac diner must call ahead and explain wheat strictly.
hiro_shizenshoku_restaurant_k.vegan_detail: A vegetable-forward natural-food kitchen using pesticide-free and organic produce, organic-rice miso, and traditional wood-barrel-fermented seasonings; the menu centers on plant-based dishes and desserts like a pesticide-free lemon cake. It is not certified fully vegan, and the daily-changing set may include fish, egg, or dairy, so confirm by phone (082-248-4221) and request a plant-only plate when you reserve.
hiro_shizenshoku_restaurant_k.notes: Kanna is a natural-food lunch restaurant on the fifth floor of the Hiroshima Ryoin wellness building, run in the spirit of the MOA natural-food movement that promotes eating in harmony with nature. chef_bio.background: Kanna is a natural-food lunch restaurant on the fifth floor of the Hiroshima Ryoin (広島療院) wellness facility in Naka-ku, run in the spirit of the MOA natural-food movement that promotes eating in harmony with nature. It is the kind of quiet, word-of-mouth place locals describe as 'known to those in the know.'
chef_bio.philosophy: Cooking that lets the ingredients speak: organic produce, organic-rice miso from Aomori made by traditional wood-barrel fermentation, and seasonings chosen without unnecessary additives.
chef_bio.specialty: A daily-changing organic lunch built around pesticide-free and organic vegetables grown by Hiroshima-area farms, finished with a homemade pesticide-free lemon cake for dessert.

anecdotes.text: The miso soup is made with organic-rice miso from Aomori, slowly aged and fermented in traditional wooden barrels, with no unnecessary additives.
Dessert features a lemon cake made with pesticide-free lemons.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog and MOA's own natural-health site confirm Kanna occupies the 5th floor of Hiroshima Ryoin (広島療院), a facility operated under MOA, which promotes natural/organic food. bm-peekaboo confirms the daily organic lunch, the Aomori organic-rice miso (wood-barrel fermented) and the pesticide-free lemon cake. Owner name not published.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: As a Japanese natural-food kitchen, miso and soy-sauce-based seasonings used here typically contain wheat; no wheat-free seasoning is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A quiet local lunch spot tucked inside a wellness building; little to no English is likely, so a translation app and a phoned-ahead plant-based request will make your visit smooth.

hiro_oshokuji_dokoro_kiraku.gf_detail: The house specialty is charcoal-grilled local anago and anagomeshi, which are glazed with a wheat-based soy-sauce tare; no gluten-free menu or dedicated handling is documented, so this is not a gluten-free destination.
hiro_oshokuji_dokoro_kiraku.vegan_detail: The menu centers on conger eel (anago), oysters and other fish-based set meals seasoned with wheat-soy sauce; no vegan or vegetarian options are documented.
hiro_oshokuji_dokoro_kiraku.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, independently run eatery on Miyajima, just off the path between the Omotesando shopping arcade and Itsukushima Shrine.

chef_bio.background: A small, independently run eatery on Miyajima (Hatsukaichi City), just off the path between the Omotesando shopping arcade and Itsukushima Shrine.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop invites visitors to try its charcoal-grilled local anago at least once.
chef_bio.specialty: Charcoal-grilled local anago (conger eel), a Miyajima specialty; anagomeshi (anago over rice) is the island's signature dish and its natural context.

anecdotes.text: The shop describes itself simply by its specialty: charcoal-grilled delicious local anago that it hopes guests will try at least once.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The Miyajima tourism association listing confirms Kiraku specializes in charcoal-grilled local anago on the shrine approach (宮島町504-2). Hitosara is only a bare listing with no menu, seat or owner detail. Owner name not published.

cultural_comfort.note: A small family-run Japanese eatery on Miyajima where some basic Japanese (or pointing at the menu) and cash will make ordering smoother, as English support is not documented.

hiro_oshokuji_dokoro_yamaichi_2.gf_detail: Not a gluten-free destination. The signature anago-meshi is glazed with a soy-sauce-based tare that contains wheat, and dishes such as tempura and grilled-oyster sauces also typically contain wheat. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented. Celiac travelers should treat this place as unsafe without direct confirmation.
hiro_oshokuji_dokoro_yamaichi_2.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The menu is built around seafood — Miyajima anago (conger eel) and oysters — and dishes use fish-based dashi and wheat-soy-based tare. No documented vegan options.
hiro_oshokuji_dokoro_yamaichi_2.hours_raw: 10:00-17:00 (official site). Some sources list 10:30-17:00 with irregular days off.

chef_bio.background: 山一本店 began not as a restaurant but as a fish market run by local Miyajima fishermen. To share the oysters and conger eel pulled from the waters around the island with the steady stream of visitors arriving by ferry, the family opened an eatery directly in front of the Miyajima pier, just a minute's walk from where the boats land.
chef_bio.philosophy: 宮島の海で獲れた新鮮な穴子と牡蠣を、訪れる人にその場で味わってもらうこと。
chef_bio.specialty: 宮島産の穴子と牡蠣を使った郷土料理。看板はあなごめしや焼き牡蠣などの穴子・牡蠣料理。

anecdotes.text: The shop traces its roots to a fish market operated by fishermen, and opened a dining room right in front of the pier so ferry arrivals could eat the day's Miyajima oysters and conger eel.

Set across multiple floors with table seating downstairs and large tatami banquet rooms above (roughly 190 seats in total), it has long served as a roomy, accessible stop for both individual travelers and tour groups near Itsukushima Shrine's approach.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Umahiro confirms Yamaichi began as a fishermen's fish market and opened a dining hall directly in front of the Miyajima pier (~1 min from the ferry) to serve local anago and oysters, with table seating downstairs and large tatami banquet rooms upstairs (2F ~80, 3F ~70; ~190 total). chef_bio.philosophy: Keeping the founder's original method unchanged and aiming for simple, natural, nostalgic flavors.

anecdotes.text: The founder created the distinctive rugby-ball melon pan because melons were an expensive luxury at the time, and he wanted ordinary people to be able to enjoy the idea of melon; the shape was inspired by makuwa-uri (Oriental melon), which was then commonly called 'melon'.
The melon pan and related products are registered trademarks, and the bakery is approaching its 90th year in business.

chef_bio.background: A casual neighborhood izakaya in central Hiroshima, a minute's walk from the Tachimachi tram stop, built around one obsession: house-made fresh gyoza. The dumplings are wrapped by hand each day for a chewy, springy skin.
chef_bio.philosophy: A play on 'health and beauty through food' — the herbs and spices folded into both the dumplings and the drinks are meant to make a hearty izakaya meal feel a little restorative.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is 薬膳生餃子 (yakuzen fresh gyoza): a pork-heavy filling worked together with an original medicinal-herb broth that is slow-simmered from roughly eight spices — star anise, dried citrus peel (陳皮), cinnamon bark (桂皮), Sichuan/flower pepper (花山椒) and more — blended with Chinese miso. Two styles are made for side-by-side tasting: 黒餃子 (with garlic and Chinese chives) and 白餃子 (without). The kitchen also turns out Hiroshima-style brothless tantanmen in three spice levels and a lineup of medicinal-herb sours.

anecdotes.text: The medicinal broth at the heart of the gyoza is cooked from about eight spices including star anise, dried citrus peel, cinnamon bark and flower pepper, then blended with Chinese miso before being worked into the pork filling, while the wrappers are folded by hand for a chewy bite.
Guests are encouraged to order both the black (garlic-and-chive) and white (no garlic or chive) gyoza to taste them against each other, alongside four signature medicinal-herb sours.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Core menu is wheat-based gyoza and wheat-noodle tantanmen, so a shared kitchen would involve heavy flour handling; no gluten-free handling is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, welcoming gyoza izakaya about a minute from the Tachimachi tram stop where solo diners are common; a little spoken Japanese helps, but pointing at the gyoza menu and a friendly "konnichiwa" will get you by.

chef_bio.background: A small counter-only yakitori shop that opened on April 3, 2023 in central Hiroshima's Tatemachi district, a few minutes' walk from the Tatemachi tram stop. The opening was actually pushed back about a week from its planned late-March date because of smoke-management issues, before the doors finally opened.
chef_bio.philosophy: The room is built as a single counter so guests sit close to the fire and take in the cooking with all five senses, the smoke, the sizzle and the aroma. The chef's attentive technique is part of the experience: misting each skewer at the start and snipping away any char with scissors mid-grill.

The chef sources different rare and regional birds by cut: prized Amakusa Daio (a long-reared Kumamoto heritage breed) for thigh and breast, offal from a Hiroshima brand chicken, and Ehime's Himekko jidori for lighter dishes like toriwasa and tataki. Signatures include sumi-grilled offal, crispy seseri (neck), creamy chi-gimo (liver), shiso-scented tsukune meatballs, hand wings cooked on iron skewers, and a closing bowl of chicken-salt ramen.

anecdotes.text: The owner previously cooked at the yakitori restaurant 'Yakitori Taniji' before opening his own counter.
Regulars note that the seats nearest the entrance are the best value because you can watch the chef's handwork up close.

anecdotes.text: Hironaka traces his love of cooking to his mother, a talented home cook, before going on to train in restaurants, a hotel, and as a group head chef, then striking out on his own in December 2017.

chef_bio.background: Gomenya is a small Hiroshima noodle operation specializing in Kure reimen, a regional cold-noodle dish born in the city of Kure. anecdotes.text: Kure reimen is presented as an independently developed regional cuisine, distinct from typical summer cold ramen or Korean naengmyeon, defined by its sweet-sour-yet-spicy sauce and springy flat noodles.

anecdotes.text: After sharing her homemade allergy-friendly sweets on social media, she received so many requests from other people with allergies that she eventually opened the café.
The shop's name 'yurumu' (to loosen / relax) reflects her wish for guests to relax body and mind over gentle, body-friendly sweets.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The kitchen bakes with domestic wheat flour, so the environment is not gluten-free and cross-contact with wheat is inherent.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The whole product line is made without eggs, dairy, or white sugar, so the kitchen does not handle those animal ingredients alongside the baked goods.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The owner started baking precisely because of her own allergy (severe atopic dermatitis) and built the shop around requests from other allergy-sufferers, so she is highly attuned to egg/dairy/white-sugar avoidance.

positives.text: Fully egg-free, dairy-free and white-sugar-free baking using beet sugar, brown rice malt syrup and soy milk — a reliable vegan-friendly sweets stop.
Prioritizes domestic, organic and pesticide-free ingredients where possible, such as organic strawberries for smoothies.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny owner-run bake café with only a few counter seats, so a little Japanese (or a translation app) helps and a friendly konnichiwa goes a long way; staff are used to allergy-conscious customers but English may be limited.

hiro_okonomimura_atomu.gf_detail: This is a Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki and teppanyaki shop. The okonomiyaki batter and the soba/udon noodles layered into it are wheat-based, and the standard okonomiyaki sauce contains wheat. No gluten-free menu, gluten-free preparation, or accommodation is documented. Not suitable for those requiring gluten-free.
hiro_okonomimura_atomu.vegan_detail: A traditional okonomiyaki house whose signature dishes contain pork, egg, and wheat noodles cooked on a shared teppan with fish/animal-based sauces. No documented vegan or vegetarian options.
hiro_okonomimura_atomu.hours_raw: 11:00–02:00 next day (food & drink L.O. 01:30 next day). Another source lists 11:00–24:00. Open daily.
hiro_okonomimura_atomu.notes: [Mom & Pop] Atomu is one of the long-running okonomiyaki stalls inside Hiroshima's famous Okonomimura, a building stacked with small okonomiyaki shops in the Shintenchi entertainment district. chef_bio.origin: Hiroshima, within the Okonomimura okonomiyaki building
chef_bio.background: Atomu is one of the long-running okonomiyaki stalls inside Hiroshima's famous Okonomimura, a building stacked with small okonomiyaki shops in the Shintenchi entertainment district. It has been serving since the 1990s and is a cozy, counter-only spot where you watch the cook work the iron griddle right in front of you.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki cooked on the teppan, including the namesake house okonomiyaki 'Atomu' made with kimchi and garlic for a hearty, stamina-packed version, plus the classic nikutama soba (pork, egg, and noodle) okonomiyaki.

anecdotes.text: The house's signature 'Atomu' okonomiyaki is loaded with kimchi and garlic for a stamina-boosting, full-flavored take on the Hiroshima classic.
Diners sit at the counter and watch the cook finish each okonomiyaki with fluid, practiced hand movements right on the griddle.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Okonomiyaki is cooked on a shared teppan griddle where wheat batter, wheat noodles, and wheat-containing sauce are all used; heavy cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Hiroshima okonomiyaki sauce is wheat-based; no gluten-free sauce is indicated.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All dishes are cooked on the same teppan used for pork, egg, and seafood, so vegan separation is not possible.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny counter-only okonomiyaki stall inside the Okonomimura food building where you sit right at the griddle; a few words of Japanese and pointing at the menu will carry you, but expect little to no English and cash only.

hiro_primevere.gf_detail: Pure fresh fruit juices and lemon soda/lemonade should be naturally gluten-free, but no allergen information is published. The savory items (rice burgers, mofles/waffle pastries) and possible seasonings cannot be assumed gluten-free. There is no dedicated gluten-free handling; a gluten-sensitive diner should stick to plain fruit juices and confirm at the counter.
hiro_primevere.vegan_detail: The fresh fruit juices (e.g., Hiroshima lemon lemonade/lemon soda, the seasonal Hiroshima Mix, pineapple frozen drinks) are fruit-based and suitable for plant-based diners. The food side (rice burgers / rice-sandwich onigiri) features conger eel (anago) and oysters, which are not vegan; the cheese-filled mofles contain dairy. Stick to the fruit juices and lemonade for a vegan-friendly choice.
hiro_primevere.hours_raw: 10:30-17:30 (official site lists 10:30-17:00; hours vary with ferry operations)
hiro_primevere.notes: [Miyajima] A small fresh-juice bar tucked along the Omotesando shopping street on Miyajima, billed as the island's only dedicated juice bar. It serves cups of juice pressed from seasonal fruit, with a signature Hiroshima Mix that changes with what is in season and Hiroshima-grown  (Map pin approximate — Omotesandō; use the Maps link for exact spot.)

chef_bio.background: A small fresh-juice bar tucked along the Omotesando shopping street on Miyajima, billed as the island's only dedicated juice bar. It serves cups of juice pressed from seasonal fruit, with a signature Hiroshima Mix that changes with what is in season and Hiroshima-grown lemon turning up in the lemonade and lemon soda. Alongside the drinks it offers Miyajima-style rice burgers and rice-wrapped onigiri.
chef_bio.philosophy: Fresh fruit juice refreshes the throat with the sweetness and acidity unique to each fruit — a vitamin pick-me-up for visitors strolling the island.
chef_bio.specialty: Fresh seasonal-fruit juices and Hiroshima-lemon drinks

anecdotes.text: Positioned as a 'vitamin charge' rest stop for Miyajima sightseers, with the tart Hiroshima-lemon soda recommended as an energizing pick for hot summer visits.
Described as Itsukushima's only juice bar, with the seasonal Hiroshima Mix as its most popular cup.

positives.text: Fresh fruit juices and Hiroshima-lemon lemonade/soda are fruit-based, giving plant-based and gluten-avoiding visitors a simple, naturally suitable option.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual walk-up juice stand on the main shopping street where pointing at the colorful fruit displays and a few words of Japanese easily get you served.

hiro_itsukushima_barl_issai.gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free program is documented. The menu centers on oysters and anago dishes such as oyster carbonara, pizza, and fried oysters, which involve wheat (pasta, dough, frying batter) and typically wheat-based soy/seasonings. A celiac or gluten-sensitive diner would need to ask carefully; nothing on the available pages confirms gluten-free preparation.
hiro_itsukushima_barl_issai.vegan_detail: Listings note a vegetarian menu is available ("ベジタリアンメニューあり"), but no detail on what those dishes are and no confirmation they are vegan. The restaurant's signature dishes are oysters, anago, and other seafood/Western fare that use fish and animal ingredients, so a strict vegan should ask in advance which specific items can be made without animal products.
hiro_itsukushima_barl_issai.hours_raw: 09:00-15:30 (L.O. 15:00), 17:00-21:00 (L.O. 20:30); closed Mondays (if Monday is a holiday, closed the following Tuesday instead)
hiro_itsukushima_barl_issai.notes: [Miyajima] 厳島BARL 厳齋 (Issai) is a casual Western-style bar and cafe that sits just about a minute's walk from the Miyajima ferry pier, making it a natural first or last stop for travelers heading to Itsukushima Shrine. It opened relatively recently as a BARL-style spot offering cr

chef_bio.background: 厳島BARL 厳齋 (Issai) is a casual Western-style bar and cafe that sits just about a minute's walk from the Miyajima ferry pier, making it a natural first or last stop for travelers heading to Itsukushima Shrine. It opened relatively recently as a BARL-style spot offering Spanish- and Italian-based Miyajima-style European cooking built on Hiroshima's signature local ingredients.
chef_bio.philosophy: A relaxed place to ease into or wind down a Miyajima visit, serving the area's prized oysters and conger eel in approachable, Western-influenced small-plate and cafe style rather than as a formal seafood restaurant.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima oysters and anago (conger eel) worked into Spanish- and Italian-based Miyajima-style European dishes - raw and grilled oysters, a popular oyster-and-mushroom ajillo, carbonara, an oyster Japanese-style pizza, and a two-kind seiro (steamed-rice) set of oyster and anago - paired with local Hiroshima sake and wine.

anecdotes.text: The kitchen reworks Hiroshima's oysters and conger eel into Spanish- and Italian-influenced bar dishes such as carbonara, an oyster Japanese-style pizza, and a signature oyster-and-mushroom ajillo, alongside raw and grilled oysters.
Positioned a one-minute walk from the Miyajima pier, it is pitched as a spot to drop into right after arriving by ferry and to relax in before heading home.

positives.text: A vegetarian menu is listed as available, so there are at least some meat-free options on offer.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, tourist-friendly spot right by the Miyajima pier where pointing at the menu and a few words of Japanese will get you by; staff are used to visitors but full English service is not confirmed.

hiro_jukeiso.gf_detail: No gluten-free program. The kitchen centers on seafood kaiseki and casual set meals (fried oysters/oyster cutlet, tempura/fried items, udon, soba, curry) that use wheat batter, wheat-based soy sauce, and shared frying. Anago-meshi and other dishes rely on soy-based seasonings. Nothing on any fetched page indicates gluten-free preparation, so GF travelers cannot rely on this kitchen.
hiro_jukeiso.vegan_detail: The inn states on its official cuisine page that vegetarian (菜食主義者) meals can be prepared with advance reservation (※事前予約要). However, this is described as vegetarian, not vegan, and no plant-only/dairy-and-egg-free detail is published. The default cuisine is heavily seafood-based (oysters, conger eel, sea bream, octopus, squid) with fish dashi and wheat-soy seasonings. A vegan would need to confirm specifics (dashi, egg, dairy) directly and book ahead.
hiro_jukeiso.hours_raw: On-site restaurant Heike lunch: 11:30–14:00, advance reservation required. Dinner kaiseki for staying guests served at 18:00 / 18:30 / 19:00 (17:30 on special-event days). Casual eatery Petit Heike: irregular hours. Inn check-in 15:00–18:00, check-out by 10:00.
hiro_jukeiso.notes: [Miyajima] Jukeiso is a traditional cuisine-ryokan founded in 1926 (Showa 1), set on a hillside overlooking Itsukushima Shrine, its great torii gate, the five-story pagoda and the treasure pagoda. Beyond lodging, it serves food: the on-site restaurant Heike offers reserved lunch c (Map pin approximate — Omotesandō; use the Maps link for exact spot.)

chef_bio.background: Jukeiso is a traditional cuisine-ryokan founded in 1926 (Showa 1), set on a hillside overlooking Itsukushima Shrine, its great torii gate, the five-story pagoda and the treasure pagoda. Beyond lodging, it serves food: the on-site restaurant Heike offers reserved lunch courses scaled to different budgets, and a casual eatery called Petit Heike at the foot of the inn — diagonally across from the Miyajima History and Folklore Museum, beside the stairway up to Jukeiso — serves everyday Miyajima fare such as anago-meshi (conger-eel rice) and grilled oysters.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house presents its cooking around the four seasons of Miyajima — spring cherry blossoms, summer breezes, autumn foliage, winter snow — aiming for encounters and emotions guests will keep in their hearts, with every dish prepared by hand for both flavor and visual beauty.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal Seto Inland Sea kaiseki built on Hiroshima oysters and anago (conger eel), alongside sea bream, yellowtail, flounder, octopus, squid and turban shells.

anecdotes.text: The inn frames Hiroshima's oysters as a point of pride, noting the region accounts for more than half of Japan's oyster production.
At the base of the inn, the old-fashioned spot Petit Heike serves anago-meshi set meals and grilled oysters, sitting just beside the staircase that climbs to Jukeiso.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Menu includes battered/fried items (fried oysters, oyster cutlet, tempura-style fried fish and shrimp, tonkatsu, fried chicken) and noodles (udon, soba), indicating shared wheat handling and frying.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes such as anago-meshi rely on standard Japanese soy-based seasonings, which are typically wheat-containing; no gluten-free seasoning is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Core kitchen is seafood-based kaiseki (oysters, conger eel, sea bream, octopus, squid) with fish-derived dashi, so shared equipment and stock are likely; a separate vegetarian menu exists only by advance request.

staff_allergy_handling.text: The inn states vegetarian meals can be prepared with prior reservation (ベジタリアン（菜食主義者）の料理もご用意可能です。※事前予約要), showing willingness to accommodate special diets when notified in advance.

positives.text: Vegetarian cuisine is offered on request with advance booking, and lunch courses are tailored to the guest's budget, suggesting flexibility for diners who communicate needs ahead of time.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a traditional family-run inn with a reserved-course dining room, so booking ahead in Japanese (by phone or through the official site) is expected and a few words of Japanese will smooth your visit.

hiro_ichinari.gf_detail: This is a Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki and teppanyaki shop. The okonomiyaki batter is wheat flour, the layered noodles (yakisoba) are wheat, and the okonomi sauce contains wheat-based soy sauce, so the core dishes are not gluten-free. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
hiro_ichinari.vegan_detail: A meat-and-egg-centric okonomiyaki/teppanyaki shop; the signature dish is 肉玉そば (pork, egg and noodles). Batter typically contains egg and dashi, and okonomi sauce is not vegan. No vegan options are documented.
hiro_ichinari.notes: [Mom & Pop] いちなり is a small okonomiyaki and teppanyaki shop run by a husband-and-wife team inside the お好み共和国ひろしま村 okonomiyaki hall, on the third floor in the Nagarekawa entertainment district of central Hiroshima. The couple relocated to this spot a few years ago and keep the place

roles: husband-and-wife owners running the shop together
chef_bio.background: いちなり is a small okonomiyaki and teppanyaki shop run by a husband-and-wife team inside the お好み共和国ひろしま村 okonomiyaki hall, on the third floor in the Nagarekawa entertainment district of central Hiroshima. The couple relocated to this spot a few years ago and keep the place open late into the night, drawing both locals and visitors after dinner.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style 肉玉そば (pork-and-egg okonomiyaki layered with noodles), cooked to order on the teppan.

anecdotes.text: Visitors single out the layered yakisoba noodles as thinner and springier than ordinary supermarket noodles, giving the okonomiyaki extra texture.
The owners are remembered as cheerful and easy to talk to; one guest recounted lingering at the counter for about three hours because the atmosphere was so welcoming.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat-based okonomiyaki batter and yakisoba noodles are cooked on a shared teppan griddle, so heavy gluten cross-contact is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Hiroshima okonomi sauce is brushed on the finished okonomiyaki and is made with wheat-based soy sauce.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Pork, egg and dashi-based ingredients are cooked together on the same griddle as all dishes.

cultural_comfort.note: A friendly, casual couple-run counter shop where the owners are described as warm and chatty, but expect mostly Japanese-only conversation, so come ready to point and smile or use a few Japanese phrases.

hiro_obanzai_rina_san_chi.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering. The core menu of obanzai, oden, and nikusui (beef broth) is built on Japanese dashi and soy sauce, which contain wheat, and there is no documentation of gluten-free preparation or accommodation.
hiro_obanzai_rina_san_chi.vegan_detail: Not vegan. Dishes rely on fish/bonito dashi and Japanese soy sauce, and the signature nikusui is a beef-broth dish; no plant-based menu is documented and there is no indication that vegan requests can be accommodated.
hiro_obanzai_rina_san_chi.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, home-style obanzai izakaya in Hiroshima's Yakkenbori nightlife quarter, opened on 22 January 2026 by owner Rina Nakagawa, who previously worked as a nurse.

chef_bio.background: A small, home-style obanzai izakaya in Hiroshima's Yakkenbori nightlife quarter, opened on 22 January 2026 by its owner, a former nurse known as Rina — the shop's name, りなさん家, means 'Rina's house.'
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner's idea is a place to unwind at the end of the day, somewhere you naturally drop by after work and feel welcomed home with a sense of tadaima.
chef_bio.specialty: Home-style obanzai (a weekly-rotating selection of seasonal side dishes), oden, and nikusui, prepared with a deeply infused dashi that one reviewer described as gently soaking into the body.

anecdotes.text: Run by a former nurse, the place is described by a guest as a shop wrapped in kindness, relaxed and unpretentious, where both mind and body unwind after a tiring day.
The weekly-rotating obanzai means there is something new to enjoy each visit, suiting both a casual drink and a proper meal.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The obanzai, oden, and nikusui menu is dashi- and soy-sauce-based; Japanese soy sauce contains wheat and there is no gluten-free preparation documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes use fish/bonito dashi and the signature nikusui is beef broth; no vegan options or separate preparation are documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 9-seat counter izakaya in a nightlife district where the warm owner makes you feel at home, but it is a late-night, Japanese-language local spot, so some basic Japanese and an easygoing attitude will help a foreign student feel comfortable.

hiro_obanzai_bar_usagi.gf_detail: No gluten-free offering or accommodation is documented. The obanzai dishes are seasoned with dashi and soy sauce (which contains wheat), and the menu includes items like macaroni salad and fresh bread, so it is not suitable for strict gluten-free diners.
hiro_obanzai_bar_usagi.vegan_detail: Not a vegan venue. The rotating obanzai spread includes meat and fish-based dishes (chicken dishes, mapo tofu, butter chicken curry) and the home-style seasoning typically relies on dashi and wheat-based soy sauce. There are several vegetable small plates (vinegared vegetables, blanched greens, braised eggplant, simmered pumpkin), but no confirmed fully plant-based preparation; a vegan diner would need to ask the owner directly.
hiro_obanzai_bar_usagi.hours_raw: 19:00–00:00 (Tue–Sat, days before holidays, etc.). Closed Sun and Mon.
hiro_obanzai_bar_usagi.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small counter bar tucked into the Mushika Building on Hiroshima's lively Mushika dori, run single-handedly by its owner, known to regulars simply as the mama. She starts cooking in the morning and prepares every dish herself, turning out a daily-changing spread of hom

chef_bio.background: A small counter bar tucked into the Mushika Building on Hiroshima's lively Mushika dori, run single-handedly by its owner, known to regulars simply as the mama. She starts cooking in the morning and prepares every dish herself, turning out a daily-changing spread of home-style obanzai.
chef_bio.philosophy: Offer warm, lovingly prepared home cooking in an intimate, hideaway setting where solo diners feel at ease.
chef_bio.specialty: All-you-can-eat handmade obanzai (Japanese home cooking) served at the counter, alongside a deep drinks list of sake, shochu and whiskey.

anecdotes.text: The owner prepares each obanzai dish one by one from the morning, and the daily lineup of eight or so small plates rotates constantly, with weekly specials such as butter chicken curry.
The counter has a hidden-gem, Kyoto-alleyway feel and a warm, home-like atmosphere that draws a loyal local crowd, including notable Hiroshima regulars.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny 9-seat counter bar run solo by the owner; you'll be most comfortable with some basic Japanese, and as a cash-only late-night spot it suits an evening sit-down rather than a quick meal.

hiro_okonomiyaki_teppanyaki_k_3.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki is built on a wheat-flour batter/crepe and noodles, and the savory dishes use standard wheat-based soy sauce and okonomiyaki sauce. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
hiro_okonomiyaki_teppanyaki_k_3.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans. The menu centers on oysters, sea urchin (ウニホーレン), beef (コウネ, A5 wagyu), pork bacon, eggs, and seafood; okonomiyaki uses egg and pork and is cooked on shared griddles with meat and fish. No vegan options are documented.
hiro_okonomiyaki_teppanyaki_k_3.hours_raw: 11:30-14:00 (L.O. 13:30) / 17:00-23:30 (L.O. 22:30), daily including holidays. Sundays may close earlier depending on customer volume. Closures are irregular.
hiro_okonomiyaki_teppanyaki_k_3.notes: A teppan izakaya in central Hiroshima a short walk from Hondori and the A-Bomb Dome, part of the local Kuraya group. The dining room blends a calm, traditional Japanese feel with private rooms, and every seat - including the counter and the tatami rooms - has its own bu

chef_bio.background: A teppan izakaya in central Hiroshima a short walk from Hondori and the A-Bomb Dome, part of the local Kuraya group. The dining room blends a calm, traditional Japanese feel with private rooms, and every seat - including the counter and the tatami rooms - has its own built-in iron griddle so food is served hot and freshly cooked right in front of you.
chef_bio.philosophy: Built around the idea that food tastes best straight off the iron plate, the restaurant fits its private griddle into every room so groups, dates, and solo diners alike can eat freshly cooked dishes; counter guests are welcomed by an easygoing owner-chef.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki cooked on the teppan alongside Seto Inland Sea seafood and griddle dishes: local oysters, the Hiroshima specialty uni horen (sea urchin on sautéed spinach), salt-grilled koune (a rare, collagen-rich wagyu beef cut), and premium A5 wagyu, all paired with local Hiroshima sake.

anecdotes.text: The menu leans into Hiroshima specialties such as uni horen (sea urchin on sautéed spinach) and salt-grilled koune, a rare collagen-rich wagyu beef cut popular with diners.
Counter seats let solo diners chat with the approachable owner-chef while their food is grilled.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Okonomiyaki, noodles, and griddle dishes share a common teppan; wheat batter and wheat-based sauces are central to the menu, so cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese soy sauce and okonomiyaki sauce (both typically wheat-containing) are used; no gluten-free sauce is mentioned.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: The page fetched completely and contains no occurrence of 醤油, ソース, たれ or any allergen statement — the only sauce-adjacent string is a dish name, 炙りネギチーズマヨ焼き. The second half ('no gluten-free sauce is mentioned') is true by absence, but the affirmative half is inferred from cuisine type, not read off

vegan_cross_contact.text: All seats use a shared iron griddle that cooks oysters, beef, pork, and seafood, so any vegetable item would contact animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A welcoming, mainstream teppan restaurant near the A-Bomb Dome where a foreign student can point at the picture menu and watch dishes cooked on the griddle, though staff communication is mostly in Japanese.

hiro_anago_meshi_kimuraya_hon.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The anago is served with sweet tare/soy-based sauce (the "black" and "red" styles) and the white style is served with a special soy sauce — Japanese soy sauce and sweet tare both contain wheat. No gluten-free menu, no allergen documentation, and the kitchen does not advertise any gluten-free handling. A celiac traveler could not eat safely here.
hiro_anago_meshi_kimuraya_hon.vegan_detail: Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. Every main is conger eel (fish), served over rice with miso soup and pickles, and even the white-grilled style uses soy sauce. There are no plant-based mains or documented meat/fish-free options.
hiro_anago_meshi_kimuraya_hon.hours_raw: Mon, Thu-Sat: 10:30-15:00 and 17:00-22:00; Wed & Sun: 10:30-15:00; Tue: closed. (Official site notes lunch-focused hours 10:30-16:00 with irregular holidays; evening izakaya service on some days.)
hiro_anago_meshi_kimuraya_hon.notes: A specialist devoted to anago-meshi, Hiroshima's century-old conger-eel-over-rice dish, set in Otemachi within sight of the A-Bomb Dome and Peace Memorial Park. The shop is run by owner Souji Kimura, who grew up around the trade — his father was a sushi chef — and the k

chef_bio.background: A specialist devoted to anago-meshi, Hiroshima's century-old conger-eel-over-rice dish, set in Otemachi within sight of the A-Bomb Dome and Peace Memorial Park. The shop is run by owner Souji Kimura, who grew up around the trade — his father was a sushi chef — and the kitchen is led by a head chef with more than twenty years of sushi experience.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner inherited from his sushi-chef father the idea of preparing every dish 'with love, just as you would cook for your own children and parents,' and the shop commits to serving food as delicious as possible using premium ingredients — pairing Hiroshima's traditional anago-meshi with refined sushi technique to create a 'new Hiroshima taste.'
chef_bio.specialty: Three contrasting styles of anago-meshi served side by side: 'black,' raw conger grilled over charcoal for a crisp, fragrant, chewy bite; 'red,' simmered then finished with a special sweet sauce until meltingly tender; and 'white,' shirayaki grilled plain to taste the eel itself, served with real wasabi and a special soy sauce. Each set comes with soup and pickles, and the chef oversees every preparation.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant frames itself as carrying forward more than 100 years of Hiroshima anago-meshi history while taking on new challenges in a place where World Heritage sites stand.
The owner says the lesson to cook 'with love just like preparing meals for our children and parents' came from his father, who was a sushi chef.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The white-style anago is served with a special soy sauce, and the black/red styles use a sweet tare; standard Japanese soy sauce and tare contain wheat.

staff_allergy_handling.text: No allergen information is published; the site provides no gluten, wheat, or cross-contamination details, so allergy diners would need to phone the shop directly.

cultural_comfort.note: An English website and menu make ordering easy for a foreign student, and the simple three-style anago format means you can just point and choose.

hiro_shirunashi_tantanmen_ich.gf_detail: This is a wheat-noodle dandan-men shop; the noodles, the meat sauce, and the seasoning base are not gluten-free, and no gluten-free option is documented. Not suitable for a strict gluten-free diet.
hiro_shirunashi_tantanmen_ich.vegan_detail: The signature bowls are built on a pork/meat sauce with sesame paste, and sets include a soft-boiled egg, so the dishes are not vegan. No vegan option is documented.
hiro_shirunashi_tantanmen_ich.notes: [Mom & Pop] This is the second shop in the Ichiraku family, the central-Hiroshima branch of a brothless dandan-noodle (汁なし担々麺) house that started in Miyoshi in northern Hiroshima. It opened in the Noboricho neighborhood on July 7, 2025.

chef_bio.background: This is the second shop in the Ichiraku family, the central-Hiroshima branch of a brothless dandan-noodle (汁なし担々麺) house that started in Miyoshi in northern Hiroshima. It opened in the Noboricho neighborhood on July 7, 2025.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cooking aims for a notably light, clean flavor rather than heavy richness; the meat sauce leans gently sweet and the sesame is present but restrained, with adjustable spice levels that stay mild.
chef_bio.specialty: Brothless dandan noodles (汁なし担々麺) served with two kinds of green onion, plus a soup version. The brothless set comes with rice and a soft-boiled egg.

anecdotes.text: Both the brothless and soup versions are described as having a characteristic lightness of flavor, with the meat sauce emphasizing sweetness and the sesame kept gentle; even at spice level 2 it reads as mild.
Staff indicated the menu is planned to expand, possibly adding mapo tofu as offered at the original Miyoshi location.

cultural_comfort.note: You order at a touch-panel ticket machine at the entrance, so a few words of Japanese and pointing will get you through comfortably even with no fluent staff English confirmed.

hiro_kiyochan.gf_detail: The ramen and tsukemen use wheat noodles and a soy-sauce-seasoned pork-bone broth, so dishes are not gluten-free and there is no gluten-free option.
hiro_kiyochan.vegan_detail: The broth is pork-bone and soy-sauce based and the bowls are topped with char siu (roast pork), so the food is not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.

chef_bio.background: Kiyochan first opened in 1973 and has served Hiroshima-style chuka soba (ramen) for around half a century. Passed down through the family, it was revived in 2018 under its third-generation owner, who carries on the shop's classic recipe.
chef_bio.philosophy: A deliberately intimate counter-only shop that has kept its traditional, minimalist approach to classic Hiroshima ramen across three generations.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style ramen and tsukemen built on an amber, gently pork-bone-scented soy-sauce broth, with medium-thin firm wheat noodles topped simply with bean sprouts, scallions, and char siu. The char siu is briefly torched before serving for a lean, savory roasted note. Wonton dishes are also offered.

anecdotes.text: The shop is so small — a counter of only about five seats — that it fills up before noon, with regulars lining up by midday.
Opened in 1973 and revived in 2018 under third-generation ownership, keeping the long-running family recipe alive.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The broth is pork-bone based and bowls are topped with char siu pork, so animal products are integral to the cooking, not just toppings.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny five-seat local counter where ordering is simple but communication is in Japanese, so a few basic words or pointing at the menu will help a foreign student feel at ease.

hiro_negian_nagarekawa_ten.vegan_detail: The menu centers on Hiroshima oysters, koune (beef neck), pork, egg, and seafood-and-wheat-based okonomiyaki, with sauces containing wheat soy sauce and likely bonito/fish stock. The kitchen describes its focus as a commitment to ingredients, noodles, and scallions.

anecdotes.text: The signature is okonomiyaki and teppanyaki heaped with locally grown Hiroshima scallions, served alongside regional teppan dishes such as oysters and koune (a collagen-rich wagyu beef cut).
A known item is a salt-and-mayo tonpei (egg-and-pork) dish the group promotes as a contest winner — taking first place nationally in the 2010 Otafuku Idea Menu Contest.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dishes are prepared on a shared griddle with pork, egg, oysters, and beef, so vegan separation is not provided.

positives.text: An English menu is available, which helps travelers identify ingredients before ordering.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu is available and solo diners are welcome, so a foreign student can comfortably order Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki and teppanyaki here even with limited Japanese.

hiro_coconca_anco_kokonka_anc.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The signature ankoronne is built on a fermented-butter puff pastry, which is wheat-based; other items (sablé, financiers) are also wheat flour confections. No gluten-free options or allergen handling were documented.
hiro_coconca_anco_kokonka_anc.vegan_detail: Not vegan. While the red bean paste (anko) itself is plant-based, the flagship ankoronne uses fermented butter pastry and a custard cream made from Brown Swiss cow's milk, so it contains dairy. Financiers and other baked goods typically contain butter and eggs. No vegan items were documented.
hiro_coconca_anco_kokonka_anc.hours_raw: 10:00–17:30 daily (one source lists 10:00–18:00); irregular days off.

chef_bio.background: 古今果anco is the casual Miyajima outpost of Fujii-ya (藤い屋), a momiji-manju and mochi maker with roughly 90 years of red-bean-paste tradition. It opened on February 25, 2017 on Miyajima's Omotesando shopping street, directly across from Fujii-ya's main shop, as an offshoot of the 'Coconca/古今果' brand the company first launched in 2015 at Miyajima-guchi as a confectionery workshop and café.
chef_bio.philosophy: A 'Japanese-Western fusion' approach to sweets, building modern pastries on the foundation of Fujii-ya's nine-decade-old traditional red bean paste so that the heritage anko is the heart of each creation.
chef_bio.specialty: Ankoronne — a coronet-shaped pastry of fermented-butter puff pastry filled with the shop's artisan anko and a custard cream made from Brown Swiss cow's milk from the Mirasaka Fromage Workshop, finished with Breton sea salt from western France.

anecdotes.text: The storefront's design echoes the Seto Inland Sea, mirroring the aesthetic of the original 2015 Coconca venue at Miyajima-guchi.
The signature ankoronne layers fermented-butter puff pastry with house anko and Brown Swiss milk custard cream, finished with Breton salt as an accent.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed counter-style sweets shop where you can point at the pastry you want and pay easily, so a few words of Japanese and gestures are plenty for a foreign student.

The signature dish layers a double egg with meat and seafood, and the sauce is a seafood-flavored Worcester-style sauce. No vegan or vegetarian dishes or modifications are documented.

chef_bio.background: Denko-Sekka is a Hiroshima okonomiyaki brand whose Ekimae Hiroba branch sits on the 6th-floor okonomiyaki theme floor (Hiroshima Okonomi Monogatari Ekimae Hiroba) of the Full Focus Building, about a three-minute walk from Hiroshima Station. The shop has grown from Hiroshima into a brand with locations across Japan.
chef_bio.philosophy: Their stated ethos is to deliver a piping-hot dish overflowing with passion and happiness ('情熱と幸せ溢れるアツアツの一枚を'), prizing the sensory experience of the teppan's heat, the aroma of the sauce, and bright, energetic service alongside quality cabbage, batter, and house sauce.
chef_bio.specialty: Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki cooked fresh on a hot teppan in front of guests. Their signature 'Denko-Sekka' okonomiyaki is known for an unusually fluffy, tender texture, layering a double egg with meat, noodles, squid tempura, shiso, and green onion.

anecdotes.text: The team describes its approach as cooking 'at full power from 10 in the morning,' with all-counter seating so guests can watch every okonomiyaki being grilled in front of them.
Beyond the classic, the kitchen offers playful original toppings, including an 'ebi-mayo' shrimp-mayonnaise version finished with a house signature sauce they say is found nowhere else.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Okonomiyaki is made from a wheat-flour batter and topped with wheat noodles, all cooked on a single shared teppan griddle alongside every other order, so cross-contact with wheat is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes are finished with okonomiyaki sauce, a wheat-based Worcester-style sauce; no wheat-free or gluten-free sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The shared griddle is used continuously for pork, egg, squid, oysters, and other animal ingredients, so any item would have animal-product cross-contact.

cultural_comfort.note: A lively, tourist-friendly okonomiyaki shop right by Hiroshima Station where you watch the cooking at a counter; a few words of Japanese help but the picture-friendly griddle experience makes ordering easy for a foreign student.

hiro_honke_soncho_no_mise.gf_detail: Hiroshima okonomiyaki is built on a wheat-flour crepe batter and wheat noodles (soba/udon) and is finished with wheat-and-soy-based okonomiyaki sauce, so the core dishes are not gluten-free. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
hiro_honke_soncho_no_mise.vegan_detail: Signature dishes contain pork, egg, squid, shrimp, oysters and cheese, and use wheat-and-soy-based sauce; the batter typically includes egg and dashi. No vegan options are documented.

chef_bio.background: GARDEN HOUSE began in Kamakura and grew into a small group of garden-side, all-day dining cafes. chef_bio.philosophy: Built around 'local sourcing (chisan-chisho)' and 'handmade,' the cafe treats the surrounding park as one large garden, aiming for a seamless connection between the dining space and nature so guests can eat amid greenery.
chef_bio.specialty: North-California-style all-day fare: hand-stretched pizza fired in a wood oven at around 450C, pasta, ricotta-cheese pancakes, and seasonal plates, paired with Japanese natural wine and Seto Inland Sea ingredients.

anecdotes.text: The design intentionally blurs the line between the restaurant and the park, framing the green space as 'a large garden' so the shop and garden feel like one continuous, nature-filled place.
The signature Bismarck pizza is built on hand-stretched dough wood-fired at about 450C for roughly a minute, topped with cream-cheese sauce, egg, cheese and prosciutto.

chef_bio.background: BioGaia TALKS is a fermented-food cafe and dialogue space in central Hiroshima's Kamiyacho district, near the A-Bomb Dome. It is run by the Swedish probiotics maker BioGaia, built around the idea that good gut health and good conversation nourish people together. The cafe's signature is yogurt made with L. reuteri lactic-acid bacteria, including a plain yogurt that faithfully recreates what is described as Japan's oldest yogurt recipe, born in the Nomura family of Hiroshima in 1917 and revived by the fifth generation.
chef_bio.philosophy: The space runs on the motto that 'knowledge is the finest entertainment,' pairing a healthy, fermentation-forward menu (kin-katsu, or 'bacteria wellness') with talk events where experts and guests share ideas face to face across medicine, science, food, and art. Greenery, a nursing room, and diaper-changing facilities make it a calm, family-friendly place to eat, read, work, or attend an event.
chef_bio.specialty: L. reuteri yogurt and smoothies, plus body-friendly fermented lunch dishes such as amazake (sweet-sake) butter chicken curry and a neba (sticky-fermented) rice bowl, available for dine-in or takeout.

anecdotes.text: The plain yogurt recreates a recipe said to be Japan's oldest, born in Hiroshima's Nomura family in 1917 and faithfully revived by the fifth generation.
A new lunch lineup featuring fermentation-based dishes like amazake butter chicken curry and a neba rice bowl launched in September 2025, available both for dine-in and takeout.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: kafe.biogaia.jpがL.ロイテリ菌ヨーグルトと1917年広島・野村家発祥『日本最古』レシピを5代目が再現と明記。goguynetが2025年9月の発酵ランチ(甘酒バターチキンカレー・ねば丼)を報道。

positives.text: The kitchen is built around fermented foods and a body-friendly, health-conscious concept, so wholesome ingredients are a stated focus.

cultural_comfort.note: A bright, modern, family-friendly cafe in central Hiroshima where a few words of Japanese help with ordering, though the casual counter-and-table setup is easy to navigate for a foreign student.
